key_takeaways: Library visitation peaked in the early 2010s (~53% of adults, ~3.85 per-capita IMLS visits in FY2019) and declined sharply during COVID-19 (2.01 per-capita in FY2022), with partial recovery by FY2024 (2.53 per-capita).
In 2022, the NEA SPPA (a Census Bureau CPS supplement) found 23% of adults visited a public library in the prior 12 months - the first time this question was asked.
Gallup (2019) found visiting the library was the most common cultural activity, averaging 10.5 visits/adult/year - more than double movie theater visits (5.3).
Women visit libraries nearly twice as often as men (Gallup: 13.4 vs 7.5; Pew: 57% vs lower for men). Low-income households visit most frequently.
Book reading has declined: 48.5% of adults read any book in 2022 (down from 54.6% in 2012). Novel/short-story reading hit a record low of 37.6%.
Print books remain dominant (64% read print in 2025 vs 31% e-book, 26% audiobook), but digital formats have grown substantially since 2011.
The main reasons for library visits are borrowing printed books (64% of visitors), reading/studying (49%), and getting help from librarians (35%).
Libraries are highly valued: 95-94% say libraries improve community quality of life; 66% say closing would majorly impact their community.
There are approximately 133,200 librarians/media collections specialists and ~402,590 core library workers (BLS OES 2024). IMLS reports 143,324 total public library staff (FY2024).

Library computer/internet access serves a critical equity role: ~23% of all Americans 16+ used library computers/internet/Wi-Fi (Pew 2016); 77 million used library computers/wireless (Gates Foundation 2010).

historical_growth.event: Library of Congress founded (April 24, 1800) with an appropriation of $5,000; initial collection of 740 books and 3 maps.
British troops burned the Capitol, destroying the Library's core collection of 3,000 volumes (August 24, 1814).
Congress approved purchase of Thomas Jefferson's personal library of 6,487 books for $23,950 (January 30, 1815).
Library moved into its own building (now the Thomas Jefferson Building), completed 1890-1897.
John Adams Building opened to the public (January 3, 1939).
James H. Billington became 13th Librarian of Congress; analog collections stood at 85.5 million items.
Analog collections exceeded 160 million items, having doubled under Billington (1987-2015).
Carla Hayden became 14th Librarian of Congress (first woman and first African American in the role).

narrative_facts: Approximately half of the Library's book and serial collections are in languages other than English; collections contain materials in some 470 languages.
The Law Library of Congress is the world's largest law library.
The Library holds the largest rare-book collection in North America, including the largest collection of 15th-century books in the Western Hemisphere.
The Geography and Map Division holds the world's largest collection of cartographic materials.
The Prints and Photographs Division contains millions of visual images.
Each working day the Library receives some 15,000 items and adds roughly 10,000 to its collections (per fascinating-facts page).

hathitrust.name: HathiTrust Digital Library
hathitrust.description: HathiTrust is a large-scale collaborative repository of digital content from research libraries and publishers worldwide. Founded by the twelve universities of the Committee on Institutional Cooperation (now the Big Ten Academic Alliance) and the University of California system, it preserves and provides access to the cultural record. Content includes items digitized by the Google Books project, Internet Archive, and local library digitization initiatives.
key_facts: 18M+ digitized volumes (Sept 2024)
6.7M volumes in the U.S. public domain
219+ member research libraries across the US, Canada, and Europe
Shared Print Program: 18M monograph volumes committed for 25-year retention
Content from Google Books, Internet Archive, and local digitization
Emergency Temporary Access Service (ETAS) provided controlled access during COVID closures
Authors Guild v. HathiTrust (2014): court upheld transformative use for accessibility and research

nlm.name: National Library of Medicine
nlm.founded: 1836 (as the Library of the Office of the Surgeon General of the Army); established as the National Library of Medicine in 1956
nlm.location: Bethesda, Maryland, United States (on the campus of the National Institutes of Health, Building 38, 8600 Rockville Pike, Bethesda, MD 20894)
nlm.type: National medical library (federal agency, institute within the National Institutes of Health)
nlm.description: The National Library of Medicine (NLM), operated by the United States federal government, is the world's largest biomedical library. Located on the campus of the National Institutes of Health in Bethesda, Maryland, NLM has been a center of information innovation since its founding in 1836. It maintains and makes available a vast print collection and produces electronic information services on a wide range of topics that are searched billions of times each year by millions of people around the globe. NLM also supports and conducts research, development, and training in biomedical informatics and health information technology, and coordinates an 8,000+ member Network of the National Library of Medicine that promotes and provides access to health information in communities across the United States.

key_databases.name: PubMed
key_databases.description: A free database primarily including the MEDLINE database of references and abstracts on life sciences and biomedical topics. Maintained by NLM at NIH as part of the Entrez system of information retrieval. First released January 1996; offered free to the public starting June 1997.
key_databases.size: More than 40 million citations and abstracts (as of March 2025)
key_databases.size_detail: 40M+ citations dating back to 1966, selectively to 1865, and highly selectively to 1809. 24.6 million records with abstracts (2023). 26.8 million records with links to full-text versions, of which 10.9 million available full-text for free (2023).

key_databases.name: MEDLINE
key_databases.description: Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online. A bibliographic database of life sciences and biomedical information covering medicine, nursing, pharmacy, dentistry, veterinary medicine, and health care. The online version of MEDLARS, launched in 1971; compiled by NLM and freely searchable via PubMed.
key_databases.size_detail: 29M+ references covering 1946-present. Updated daily with 2,000-4,000 references per update. Covers 40 languages for current journals, 60 for older journals. Over 93% of records are published in English.
key_databases.history: MEDLARS launched 1964 as first large-scale computer-based retrospective search service; online version (MEDLINE) began late 1971

key_databases.name: PubMed Central (PMC)
key_databases.description: A free digital repository that archives openly accessible full-text scholarly articles published in biomedical and life sciences journals. More than a document repository - submissions are indexed and formatted for enhanced metadata, medical ontology, and unique identifiers. A major research database developed by NCBI.
key_databases.history: Began as E-biomed, proposed May 1999 by then-NIH director Harold Varmus. Hosts access to human genome (2000). 2008 NIH Public Access Policy mandated NIH-funded research be available on PMC within 12 months of publication.

key_databases.name: ClinicalTrials.gov
key_databases.description: A registry of clinical trials run by NLM at NIH. Launched February 29, 2000 following the Food and Drug Administration Modernization Act of 1997. Expanded by FDA Amendments Act of 2007 to require registration and results reporting.

key_databases.name: National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI)
key_databases.description: An intramural division within NLM that creates public databases in molecular biology, conducts research in computational biology, develops software tools for analyzing molecular and genomic data, and disseminates biomedical information. Founded November 4, 1988 through legislation sponsored by Congressman Claude Pepper.
key_databases.size: Houses multiple major databases including GenBank, PubMed, PMC, and dozens of others

key_databases.name: GenBank
key_databases.description: An open access, annotated collection of publicly available nucleotide sequences and their protein translations. Part of the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC). Produced and maintained by NCBI at NLM/NIH. Established in 1982 by Walter Goad at Los Alamos National Laboratory.
key_databases.size: 53.90 trillion bases in 6.27 billion sequence records (release 271, April 2026)
key_databases.size_detail: Traditional GenBank entries: 261,460,182 records containing 7,289,942,983,522 base pairs (April 2026). Combined with WGS: 45,628,511,953,497 bases in 4,756,526,485 sequences. Includes sequences from more than 581,000 formally described species. Doubles approximately every 18 months.

key_databases.name: MedlinePlus
key_databases.description: An online consumer health information service produced by NLM. Provides curated consumer health information in English and Spanish with select content in additional languages. Brings together information from NLM, NIH, other U.S. government agencies, and health-related organizations. Introduced October 1998.
key_databases.size: Almost 1,000 health topics in English and Spanish, with links to health information in over 40 languages

key_databases.name: MeSH (Medical Subject Headings)
key_databases.description: The NLM controlled vocabulary thesaurus used for indexing articles for PubMed/MEDLINE. A comprehensive life science vocabulary that enables consistent retrieval of biomedical literature.

key_databases.name: ChemIDplus
key_databases.description: A chemical database of over 400,000 chemicals complete with names, synonyms, and structures. Includes links to NLM and other databases and resources, including federal, state, and international agencies.

key_databases.name: LocatorPlus
key_databases.description: NLM's online catalog, providing access to the library's collection holdings.

key_databases.name: TOXNET (Toxicology Data Network)
key_databases.description: Toxicology and environmental health information system established at NLM in 1967. Includes databases compiled from medical literature and governmental/nongovernmental organization files for chemical emergency response and public education.
key_databases.related_resources: TOXMAP, Tox Town, Wireless Information System for Emergency Responders, Toxmystery, Household Products Database

key_databases.name: Unified Medical Language System (UMLS)
key_databases.description: A set of files and software that brings together many health and biomedical vocabularies and standards to enable interoperability between computer systems. NLM is the U.S. National Release Center for SNOMED CT.

nnlm_network.name: Network of the National Library of Medicine (NNLM)
nnlm_network.description: NNLM is coordinated by 14 institutions across the United States. Member organizations provide health professionals and the general public with health information resources and services. The network promotes and provides access to health information in communities across the United States.

historical_timeline.event: Founded as the Library of the Office of the Surgeon General of the Army with $150 for medical books; first catalog of books issued in 1840
Library moved to Riggs Bank Building at 15th Street and Pennsylvania Avenue, NW, Washington, DC
Lieutenant John Shaw Billings appointed to take charge of the collection, marking a turning point in the library's development
Library moved to Ford's Theatre (after Lincoln's assassination) at 513 10th Street NW, Washington, DC; remained until 1887
Billings began Index Medicus, the first comprehensive index of journal articles; predecessor to MEDLINE
Index-Catalogue launched, a combined author and subject catalog of the library's growing collection
Library moved to Army Medical Museum and Library Building at 7th Street and Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC (remained until 1962)
By Billings' departure, holdings reached 116,847 books and 191,598 pamphlets; transformed into the world's greatest medical library
Officially renamed the Army Medical Library
Library transferred from Department of Defense to the Public Health Service and renamed the National Library of Medicine via Public Law 941 (August 3, 1956)
Library took first steps into the computer age, launching a mechanized system for producing its publications
Library moved to its current quarters on the NIH campus in Bethesda, Maryland
MEDLARS (Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System) launched as the first large-scale, computer-based retrospective search service available to the general public; cost $3 million to develop
Toxicology and Environmental Health Program established at NLM
MEDLINE (MEDLARS Online) became available for online searching from remote medical libraries; initially covered 239 journals
Director Donald Lindberg's Grateful Med project facilitated direct, affordable access to the MEDLINE database
National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) established within NLM (November 4, 1988) through legislation by Congressman Claude Pepper
NCBI team developed the BLAST tool for comparing biological sequences
NCBI established a website for online access to BLAST, GenBank, and the Entrez retrieval system
PubMed first released in January 1996, ushering in free home and office-based MEDLINE searching
PubMed offered free to the public starting June 1997
MedlinePlus introduced in October 1998 to provide consumer-friendly health information
PubMed Central launched; ClinicalTrials.gov made available to the public on February 29, 2000; NCBI hosted access to the human genome
Last printed issue of Index Medicus published in December 2004, replaced by freely accessible PubMed
FDA Amendments Act of 2007 mandated expansion of ClinicalTrials.gov for tracking basic results of clinical trials
NIH Public Access Policy mandated that NIH-funded research papers be made available on PubMed Central within 12 months of publication
Stephen Sherry selected as Acting Director of NLM (October 1, 2023) following retirement of Patricia Flatley Brennan

ill.title: Interlibrary Loan (ILL) Statistics Summary
ill.source: Primary quantitative source: IMLS Public Libraries Survey (PLS), FY2000-FY2024, fields LOANFM (loans from / borrowed) and LOANTO (loans to / lent), parsed by scripts/parse_pls_historical.py into data/pls_trends_national.csv and data/pls_trends_by_state.csv. Raw PLS vintages cached under data/_cache/pls_historical/ (FY2000-FY2023) and data/_cache/pls_fy2024_csv.zip (FY2024); FY2024 download URL https://www.imls.gov/sites/default/files/2026-06/pls_fy2024_csv.zip. OCLC and network statistics drawn from OCLC product/about pages (resource-sharing, Tipasa, WorldShare ILL, ILLiad, annual report) and the Wikipedia articles on OCLC, Interlibrary loan, the Center for Research Libraries, and the Association of Research Libraries, all cached under data/_cache/ill_*. State-level and Maine InfoNet details from maineinfonet.org and crl.edu. ARL Statistics referenced from arl.org/arl-terms/arl-statistics/ (latest edition ARL Statistics 2024, 124 U.S. member libraries); ARL transaction-level tables are paywalled and not freely available online. ALA Interlibrary Loan Code for the United States is maintained by the RUSA STARS committee (ala.org/rusa); ALA's CMS returned 404 boilerplate for the tested URLs during this fetch, so the code is cited as a known standard rather than from cached live text. WebFetch calls against several sites (ARL, ALA, OCLC, study repositories) repeatedly timed out or returned 400/403/404; quantitative figures were therefore extracted directly from the curl-cached HTML in data/_cache/ill_* via local text parsing.

trend_summary.note: Earliest PLS vintage in this dataset; modest ILL volume.
Rapid growth phase: borrowed rose from 16.3M to 55.5M (+241%) as OCLC resource sharing became ubiquitous and ILLiad workflows matured.
Plateau/peak era; total ILL transactions peaked at ~141.5M in FY2013 (borrowed 70.7M, lent 70.8M).
Flat at ~140M total; first signs of softening as e-book and digital-licensing access began substituting for some returnable ILL.
Notable step-down to 128.5M (from 140.8M in 2016, -8.7%), the first sharp decline -- coincides with maturation of statewide e-book platforms and ebook lending.
COVID-19 disruption: fell to 99.7M total (-29.5% from FY2013 peak; -27.3% vs FY2019) as buildings closed and physical shipping halted.
Recovery: rebounded to 130.1M (2021), dipped to 118.3M (2022), 123.1M (2023), and 137.3M (2024) -- essentially back to pre-pandemic levels but still below the 2013 peak.
FY2024 borrowed (70.74M) exceeded FY2013's borrowed total, making FY2024 the highest borrowed-year on record; lent (66.6M) remained below the 2013 lent peak.
Over 24 years borrowed grew +335% and lent +305%, but most growth occurred 2000-2013; the 2017-2022 era shows structural softening partly offset by 2024 recovery.

networks.name: OCLC Resource Sharing Network
networks.description: World's largest ILL network; the backbone of U.S. and global interlibrary loan. Lenders/borrowers are matched through the WorldCat union catalog. Successor products Tipasa and WorldShare ILL replaced the legacy OCLC ILL messaging service.

networks.name: RapidILL
networks.description: Unmediated, automated ILL/document-delivery system developed at Colorado State University in 1997 after the Spring Creek flood destroyed journal holdings. Known for very fast turnaround and high automation. Acquired by Ex Libris in 2019 and now offered alongside Rapido.

networks.name: Libraries Very Interested in Sharing (LVIS)
networks.description: An OCLC resource-sharing 'group' whose members agree to lend to one another for free (no per-transaction fee), reducing ILL costs among participants.

networks.name: OCLC Express
networks.description: An OCLC program for libraries that commit to 18-hour-or-less turnaround; Express libraries receive priority routing of copy requests.

networks.name: Center for Research Libraries (CRL)
networks.description: A global consortium of university, college and research libraries (75+ years) that operates a buy-in shared-collection model; members borrow from CRL's deep holdings of newspapers, foreign dissertations, archival microforms, and rare materials not held elsewhere.

networks.name: Research Libraries Group (RLG)
networks.description: Former major academic-library resource-sharing network (RLG ILL) and union catalog (RLIN). Merged into OCLC in July 2006; its user base was folded into the OCLC resource-sharing network.

networks.name: Maine InfoNet
networks.description: Maine's statewide library network. Operates MaineCat (a statewide union catalog combining 100+ library collections in 10 large online systems), Minerva (a shared ILS for 60+ libraries of all types), URSUS/MILS (shared catalogs), and the Download Library / Digital Maine Library (shared e-book/e-audio collection).

networks.name: National Network of Libraries of Medicine (NNLM) / DOCLINE
networks.description: The U.S. medical-library resource-sharing network coordinated by the National Library of Medicine. NLM developed DOCLINE, a specialized request-routing system for biomedical document delivery among NNLM member libraries.

networks.name: Amigos Library Services
networks.description: Regional library cooperative (successor to AMIGOS Bibliographic Council) providing OCLC billing/cataloging support and resource-sharing services to member libraries, primarily in the Southwest.

networks.name: State-level consortia / backbones
networks.description: Many of the highest-ILL states owe their volume to statewide consortial backbones: OhioLINK (OH), WiLS (WI), Massachusetts Library System (MA), Empire State Library Network/NY3Rs (NY), ILDS/ILLINET (IL), PALCI (PA), MCLS (MI), CARLI (IL academic), etc. These route intra-state requests cheaply, inflating PLS ILL counts relative to states that rely on direct OCLC requests.

oclc_stats.organization: OCLC (Online Computer Library Center), Dublin, Ohio
oclc_stats.legal_status: 501(c)(3) nonprofit member cooperative; renamed OCLC, Inc. in 2017
oclc_stats.resource_sharing_network_size: 10,000+ libraries in 50+ countries (largest such network in the world)
oclc_stats.e_resource_requests_per_year: 3,000,000+ e-resource requests delivered through the OCLC network each year (WorldShare ILL)
oclc_stats.daily_search_requests: 40+ million search requests processed each day by OCLC systems (all discovery, not ILL-specific)
oclc_stats.express_program: 1,000+ libraries participate in OCLC Express; copy requests filled in an average of 10 hours; e-resources sometimes delivered in as little as 15 minutes
oclc_stats.lvis_group: Libraries Very Interested in Sharing (LVIS) -- 2,200 participants that lend to one another for free

products.name: Tipasa
products.description: Cloud-based ILL management system; connects to 10,000+ libraries in 50+ countries; patron interface in 18 languages; ISO 18626 compliant; successor to ILLiad for many libraries.

products.name: WorldShare Interlibrary Loan
products.description: Cloud-based borrowing/lending automation on the WorldShare platform; delivered 3M+ e-resource requests/year; some e-resources delivered in 15 minutes.

products.name: ILLiad
products.description: Legacy locally-hosted ILL management software (Atlas Systems / OCLC); still operated by many libraries; managed 24/7 by hosting teams.

products.name: OCLC Resource Sharing for Groups
products.description: Modern consortial borrowing platform for groups/consortia.

products.name: Relais ILL / D2D
products.description: Acquired by OCLC in 2017 (Relais International, Ottawa); supports direct-to-document and consortial document delivery.

products.name: RapidILL
products.description: Originally developed at Colorado State University in 1997; acquired by Ex Libris in 2019; 300+ member libraries internationally, most in the U.S. Now part of Ex Libris' Rapido/RapidILL resource-sharing line.

academic_libraries_arl.source: Association of Research Libraries (ARL) Statistics, published annually since 1963 (ARL assumed responsibility for annual library statistics that year).
academic_libraries_arl.latest_publication: ARL Statistics 2024 (published 2025), describing collections, staffing, expenditures and service activities of 124 ARL member libraries in the U.S. (plus Canadian members reported separately).
academic_libraries_arl.metrics_tracked: ARL Statistics include interlibrary loan (borrowed and lent) and document delivery as distinct service metrics for research libraries -- the returnable (book) vs non-returnable (document/article) split is captured here rather than in IMLS PLS.
academic_libraries_arl.access_note: ARL Statistics tables are a member/paywalled publication; transaction-level totals are not freely available online. IMLS PLS (this file) covers public libraries only, so academic ILL volume is NOT included in the national_totals above.

document_delivery_vs_book_breakdown.summary: IMLS PLS does NOT split returnable (physical book) from non-returnable (document/article) ILL; both are counted together in LOANFM/LOANTO. The split is tracked by OCLC (Tipasa/WorldShare ILL) and ARL Statistics.
document_delivery_vs_book_breakdown.oclc_e_resource_requests_per_year: 3,000,000+ (OCLC WorldShare ILL) -- a proxy for non-returnable / document-delivery volume through OCLC.
document_delivery_vs_book_breakdown.oclc_physical_loans_estimate: The bulk of the ~140M annual PLS transactions are returnable physical loans (books/media shipped between public libraries), since public-library ILL is dominated by print monographs; OCLC's 3M+ e-resource figure is a small fraction of total public-library ILL.
document_delivery_vs_book_breakdown.trend_note: Over time the share of non-returnable (article/document delivery) has fallen as more journal content is licensed directly via database subscriptions; conversely, e-book and digital-audio circulation (316M ebook + 245M e-audio circulations in FY2024 per IMLS PLS digital file) now substitutes for some returnable book ILL -- one structural reason ILL plateaued 2014-2017.

digital_resource_context_fy2024.source: IMLS PLS FY2024 electronic-services data (this project's data/pls_fy2024_digital.json)
digital_resource_context_fy2024.interpretation: Public libraries circulated ~555M electronic items in FY2024 -- roughly 4x the total national ILL volume (137M). The expansion of direct e-licensing and statewide shared e-book platforms is the main structural pressure reducing growth in returnable book ILL, even as overall ILL has recovered post-COVID.

definitions.loans_borrowed: Items a library received FROM other libraries via ILL (IMLS PLS field LOANFM). Also called 'borrowed' or 'received'.
definitions.loans_lent: Items a library supplied TO other libraries via ILL (IMLS PLS field LOANTO). Also called 'lent' or 'supplied'.
definitions.returnable_vs_nonreturnable: Industry distinguishes 'returnable' loans (physical books/media shipped back) from 'non-returnable' / document delivery (article scans, chapter PDFs). IMLS PLS counts both in LOANFM/LOANTO without splitting the two; the returnable/non-returnable split is tracked in OCLC/Tipasa and ARL Statistics.

key_facts: U.S. public libraries reported 137,344,470 interlibrary-loan transactions in FY2024 (70.74M borrowed, 66.60M lent) -- IMLS Public Libraries Survey.
ILL peaked at ~141.5M total transactions in FY2013, dipped during COVID to 99.7M in FY2020 (-29.5% from peak), and recovered to 137.3M by FY2024.
FY2024 set the record for 'borrowed' (materials received via ILL) at 70.74M, surpassing FY2013; 'lent' (66.6M) remained below the 2013 peak of 70.8M.

Over 24 years (FY2000->FY2024) total public-library ILL grew +318% (borrowed +335%, lent +305%), but nearly all growth occurred 2000-2013; the post-2013 era shows plateau/decline partly offset by post-COVID recovery.

OCLC operates the world's largest resource-sharing network: 10,000+ libraries in 50+ countries, delivering 3M+ e-resource ILL requests per year; OCLC itself has ~30,000 member libraries in 100+ countries.
OCLC's Express program (1,000+ libraries) fills copy requests in an average of 10 hours; some e-resource requests deliver in 15 minutes.
LVIS (Libraries Very Interested in Sharing), an OCLC free-lending group, has 2,200 participating libraries.
RapidILL, an automated unmediated ILL system developed at Colorado State University in 1997, has 300+ member libraries and was acquired by Ex Libris in 2019.
The ALA Interlibrary Loan Code for the United States (maintained by RUSA STARS, first national code 1917, current revision 2016) governs U.S. ILL practice.
Research Libraries Group (RLG) merged into OCLC in July 2006, consolidating U.S. academic-library resource sharing onto the OCLC network.
Ohio is the #1 ILL state by volume (FY2024: 8.76M borrowed, 8.75M lent) thanks to the OhioLINK consortium backbone; Wisconsin, Massachusetts, New York and Illinois round out the top 5.

Academic-library ILL is tracked separately by the ARL Statistics (124 U.S. ARL member libraries, latest edition ARL Statistics 2024) and captures the returnable-vs-document-delivery split that IMLS PLS does not.

IMLS PLS does NOT separate returnable (physical book) from non-returnable (document/article) ILL; both are counted in the LOANFM/LOANTO totals. OCLC reports 3M+ e-resource (largely non-returnable) requests/year as a partial proxy.
Public libraries circulated ~555M electronic items (ebooks, e-audio, e-video) in FY2024 -- about 4x the national ILL volume -- illustrating how direct e-licensing now substitutes for some ILL demand.
The borrowed/lent ratio has stayed near 1.0 for two decades (FY2024: 1.06), reflecting that ILL is a reciprocal exchange: libraries borrow roughly as much as they lend.
methodology_and_caveats: national_totals and by_state are computed directly from IMLS Public Libraries Survey microdata (FY2000-FY2024), fields LOANFM and LOANTO, in this project's data/pls_trends_national.csv and data/pls_trends_by_state.csv (generated by scripts/parse_pls_historical.py).

PLS covers U.S. public library administrative entities only (9,249 systems in FY2024). Academic, special, school, and medical libraries are excluded -- so the national total UNDERCOUNTS total U.S. ILL activity.
PLS uses negative sentinels (-1/-3/-9) for missing data; these are treated as zero/missing in aggregation, so a few non-reporting systems contribute 0 (a slight undercount).
OCLC figures are self-reported by OCLC on its product/about pages and the OCLC Wikipedia article (citing OCLC's 2020-21 annual report); they describe the global network, not U.S.-only volume.
ARL Statistics (academic research libraries) is a paywalled publication; exact academic ILL transaction counts were not freely retrievable online and are therefore referenced qualitatively.
The returnable vs non-returnable (document delivery) split is not available in PLS; the breakdown here is inferred from OCLC's 3M+ e-resource figure and industry knowledge, not a direct PLS count.
ill.verification: Verified FY2024 totals against pls_extended_metrics.json: borrowed matches, lent matches. Normalized into requested summary structure without losing detail.

library_workforce.total_employed_note: Sum of BLS OEWS employment across 4 library occupations (25-4022, 25-4031, 43-4111, 25-1082); librarians alone (25-4022) = 133,200. DPE/AFL-CIO 2016 fact sheet reported 295,000 across librarians+technicians+assistants in 2015.

gender_breakdown.source: AFL-CIO Department for Professional Employees, 'Library Workers: Facts & Figures 2016' (83% women in 2015) and Wikipedia/Librarian citing 2019 data (81% women, 79% in 2018). Library Journal 2023 Placements & Salaries Survey (class of 2022): 74% women, 18% male, 6% nonbinary/gender nonconforming, 2% undisclosed among new MLIS graduates.
gender_breakdown.notes: Librarianship has been majority-female since ~1930; women were 80% of the profession by 1960. Share has held at ~80-84% for decades.

racial_ethnic.source: AFL-CIO DPE 'Library Workers: Facts & Figures 2016' citing BLS/CPS 2015 data for librarians. Library assistants were more diverse: 74% non-Hispanic White in 2015. Library Journal 2023 Placements & Salaries Survey (class of 2022 new MLIS graduates): 74% white, 10% Asian (7% South Asian, 2% East Asian, 1% Southeast Asian), 8% Hispanic/Latine, 4% Black/African American, 3% mixed race, 2% Native American/Indigenous, 5% undisclosed — white share down from 84% in 2021.
racial_ethnic.notes: The librarian profession has a persistent racial diversity lag; workforce is far whiter than the broader U.S. labor force. Diversity is greater among library technicians/assistants and improving among new MLIS graduates.

library_workforce.age_distribution_note: Average age of new MLIS graduates (class of 2022) was 35, unchanged from 2021. The overall librarian workforce skews older: 42% of librarians were over 55 in 2014 (DPE), signaling an aging workforce and impending retirements.

education.source: AFL-CIO DPE 'Library Workers: Facts & Figures 2016' citing 2014 data. Among librarians: 55% held a master's degree or higher (typically the ALA-accredited MLIS), 26% reported a bachelor's as their highest degree. Library technicians: 16% bachelor's, 8% master's, 6% associate's. Library assistants: 23% bachelor's, 6% master's, 10% associate's.
education.mlis_context: The Master of Library and Information Science (MLIS) from an ALA-accredited program is the terminal professional degree required for most librarian positions in the U.S. and Canada. Library Journal 2023 survey: 37 ALA-accredited institutions graduated the class of 2022; 81% had no advanced degree prior to starting their LIS program; 91% were not enrolled in another graduate program.

union_membership.source: AFL-CIO DPE 'Library Workers: Facts & Figures 2016' citing BLS Current Population Survey 2015. Education, training, and library occupations had the HIGHEST unionization rate of any professional occupation group (35.5%).
union_membership.union_wage_premium: Union librarians earned 37% ($336) more per week than non-union counterparts in 2015. Union library assistants earned 99% more than non-union counterparts. Union library technicians earned 49% more (last comparable data 2009).

library_workforce.by_state_note: BLS OEWS employment for SOC 25-4022 (Librarians and Media Collections Specialists) by state. Top states by employment: New York (11,020), California (10,030), Texas (9,430), Florida (5,960), Pennsylvania (5,420). Includes DC, Puerto Rico, and Virgin Islands.

gender_wage_gap.source: AFL-CIO DPE 2016 (2014 data); Wikipedia/Librarian (2019 data); Library Journal 2023 Placements & Salaries Survey (2022 graduates). Gender pay gap among new MLIS graduates narrowed from 15.5% (2021) to 9% (2022).

racial_wage_gap_2015_cents_per_dollar_ea.source: AFL-CIO DPE 2016 citing 2015 BLS data. 2019 figures (Wikipedia/Librarian): African American women 69.9 cents, Hispanic/Latina women 63.8 cents, Asian women 76.7 cents vs Asian men.

racial_wage_gap_higher_ed_2014.source: AFL-CIO DPE 2016: Black full-time librarians in higher education earned 90% of White counterparts in 2014.

library_technicians_gender_gap_2014.note: High margin of error due to few men in the sample.

key_facts: The U.S. library workforce comprises ~370,560 workers across four BLS occupational categories (2023 OEWS): 133,200 librarians/media collections specialists, 159,620 library assistants, 74,080 library technicians, and 3,660 postsecondary library science teachers.

Librarianship is one of the most female-dominated professions in the U.S.: women were 83% of librarians in 2015 (DPE) and 81% in 2019; the share has held at roughly 80-84% since the 1990s. Among new 2022 MLIS graduates, 74% were women, 18% men, 6% nonbinary/gender nonconforming (LJ 2023).

The profession has a persistent racial diversity gap: 84% of librarians were non-Hispanic White in 2015, vs. 74% of library assistants. Among new 2022 MLIS graduates the white share fell to 74% (from 84% in 2021), with Asian graduates rising to 10% — a notable diversification trend among new entrants.
The workforce is aging: 42% of librarians were over age 55 in 2014, signaling a wave of impending retirements and succession challenges. New MLIS graduates average age 35 (2022).

Despite being female-dominated, a gender wage gap persists: women full-time librarians earned 93% of men's median salary in 2014 ($48,589 vs $52,528) and 92% in 2019. The gap is wider for women of color — African American women earned 69-70 cents and Hispanic/Latina women 63-64 cents per dollar earned by men (2015/2019).

Education, training, and library occupations had the HIGHEST unionization rate of any professional occupation group in 2015 (35.5%). 20.5% of librarians, 16.3% of library assistants, and 11.2% of library technicians were union members. Union librarians earned 37% more per week than non-union counterparts.

Cumulative employment among librarians, technicians, and assistants shrank from 380,000 (2007) to 295,000 (2015) — a 22.5% decline. Employment of elementary/secondary school librarians fell 25% (2004-2014), from ~80,000 to ~66,000.

The average full-time starting salary for new MLIS graduates was $61,473 in 2022 (LJ 2023 survey), up from $45,650 in 2013 but with a COVID dip to $56,453 in 2020. Unemployment among new graduates fell to 5% in 2023 from 7% in 2022.

ALA's Spectrum Scholarship Program awards scholarships to minority library students to diversify the profession; ALA provides over $300,000 in scholarships annually. In 2022 ALA formally acknowledged its history of 'upholding unjust systems of racism and discrimination against Black, Indigenous, and People of Color (BIPOC)' and resolved to build a more equitable association.

The MLIS (Master of Library and Information Science) from an ALA-accredited program is the terminal professional degree for librarians in the U.S. and Canada; 55% of librarians held a master's degree or higher in 2014. Most academic librarians also hold a second subject-based master's degree.

Health insurance coverage in 2014: 80% of librarians had employer/union health insurance (4% uninsured), but only 63% of library technicians (8% uninsured) and 66% of library assistants (9% uninsured) — reflecting poorer benefits for paraprofessional staff.

employment_by_sector.source: AFL-CIO DPE 2016 fact sheet. 'Special libraries' includes businesses, law firms, nonprofits, and scientific organizations.

ala_diversity_initiatives.spectrum_scholarship: ALA's Spectrum Scholarship Program awards academic scholarships to minority library students each year to diversify the profession. ALA provides over $300,000 in scholarships annually across its programs.
ala_diversity_initiatives.office_for_diversity_literacy_outreach: The ALA Office for Diversity, Literacy and Outreach Services (ODLOS) supports library/information workers in creating inclusive spaces, using a social justice framework.
ala_diversity_initiatives.2022_bipoc_acknowledgment: In 2022 ALA expanded its accountability to include the organization's history of 'upholding unjust systems of racism and discrimination against Black, Indigenous, and People of Color (BIPOC) within the association and the profession' and resolved to build a more equitable association.
ala_diversity_initiatives.committee_on_status_of_women: ALA's Committee on the Status of Women in Librarianship (COSWL), founded 1976, promotes collection/analysis of information on the status of women in librarianship.
ala_diversity_initiatives.source: Wikipedia/American Library Association and archived ALA Office for Diversity page (Wayback Machine, 2020 snapshot).

workforce_challenges.declining_employment: Cumulative library employment (librarians+technicians+assistants) fell 22.5%, from 380,000 in 2007 to 295,000 in 2015 (DPE). School librarian employment fell 25% from 2004 to 2014 (80,000 to 66,000); library technician employment fell 50% and library assistant employment fell 30% over the same period.
workforce_challenges.aging_workforce: 42% of librarians were over age 55 in 2014, indicating large-scale pending retirements and a need for succession planning and recruitment.
workforce_challenges.new_graduate_job_market: Library Journal's 2023 survey found 5% unemployment among 2022 MLIS graduates (down from 7%); 87% of employed graduates held full-time positions; 19% worked outside the library field. Employers emphasize prior experience, creating an 'experience needed to get experience' barrier for new graduates.
workforce_challenges.diversity_recruitment: The profession remains far less racially diverse than the U.S. population; ALA's Spectrum Scholarship and other initiatives target minority recruitment, and new-graduate cohorts are diversifying (white share fell from 84% in 2021 to 74% in 2022).
workforce_challenges.source: AFL-CIO DPE 'Library Workers: Facts & Figures 2016'; Library Journal 2023 Placements & Salaries Survey.

library_workforce.source_notes: Primary employment, wage, and by-state data: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS), SOC 25-4022 (Librarians and Media Collections Specialists), 25-4031 (Library Technicians), 43-4111 (Library Assistants, Bookkeeping, Clerical), and 25-1082 (Library Science Teachers, Postsecondary) — May 2023 reference data, published 2024; cached locally at data/bls_librarian_salaries.json (BLS site blocks automated retrieval). gates_foundation.description: Introduced a U.S. Libraries initiative in 1997 with the goal of connecting public libraries to the internet. The foundation gave grants, installed computers and software, and provided training and technical support in partnership with public libraries nationwide to increase access and knowledge, helping move public libraries into the digital age. The international Global Libraries program extended this work to public libraries outside the U.S.
gates_foundation.scope_us: Reached public library systems across all 50 U.S. states with computers, internet access, and training.

private_giving_to_libraries.total_annual_estimate: No single authoritative figure publishes total annual private giving to all US libraries. IMLS and ALA track public funding (local/state/federal) but private/donated revenue is reported inconsistently. A meaningful share of private support flows through Friends groups (thousands nationally), library foundations, and endowment income.
private_giving_to_libraries.note: Public libraries derive ~80-90% of revenue from local government (per IMLS PLS); private giving supplements this for programming, collections, and capital projects. Candid (Foundation Center/Candid) tracks foundation grants to libraries but no single national total is published.

crowdfunding_and_community_fundraising.friends_groups_book_sales: Used-book sales are a major revenue source for thousands of Friends of the Library groups; book sales can be major community events. Friends also receive book donations to resell.
crowdfunding_and_community_fundraising.membership_drives: Annual membership drives are a primary fundraising method for Friends groups (membership fees/donations).
crowdfunding_and_community_fundraising.library_retail_shops: Some Friends groups sell items in retail space inside the libraries they support (e.g., Friends of the Library Shop at Salt Lake City Main Library).
crowdfunding_and_community_fundraising.capital_campaigns: Some Friends groups formed specifically to build new libraries (e.g., Naples, FL Friends formed 1957 to build Collier County library; accepted donated land leased to the city).
crowdfunding_and_community_fundraising.statewide_friends_groups: State-level Friends organizations coordinate advocacy and fundraising across local groups (statewide groups began forming in the 1960s).
crowdfunding_and_community_fundraising.modern_crowdfunding: Platforms such as GoFundMe, Kickstarter, and DonorsChoose are used by libraries and Friends groups for project-specific campaigns; ALA and United for Libraries provide fundraising toolkits (e.g., Citizens-Save-Libraries Power Guide). No single published total for library crowdfunding exists.
crowdfunding_and_community_fundraising.ala_toolkits: ALA/United for Libraries provide toolkits, factsheets, listservs, free toolkits, and contact information for State Friends Groups to support local fundraising and advocacy.

adopt_a_book_programs.description: Adopt-a-Book programs allow donors to sponsor the purchase or conservation of specific library books, often with bookplates recognizing the donor. Run by individual libraries, their Friends groups, and affiliated foundations.

Promotes Adopt-a-Book and similar donor programs among member Friends groups and foundations via awards, grants, and resources.

adopt_a_book_programs.similar_programs: Many public and academic libraries run 'Adopt-a-Book,' 'Buy-a-Book,' and sponsor-a-shelf programs through their Friends groups or foundations; details vary by institution and are not centrally tallied.
adopt_a_book_programs.source: Wikipedia: Smithsonian Libraries; ALA United for Libraries

key_facts: Andrew Carnegie funded 2,509 libraries worldwide (1883-1929), including 1,689 in the United States, at a cost of ~$56.2 million (~$40 million for 1,670 US public library buildings in 1,412 communities).
By the time of Carnegie's last library grant, he had funded construction of nearly half of the 3,500 libraries then in the United States.
The first US Friends of the Library group was founded in 1922 in Glen Ellyn, Illinois; the first university Friends group at Harvard in 1925.
By 1973 there were ~1,000 Friends groups with over 100,000 members; by 1979 (at FOLUSA's formation) ~2,000 groups with ~500,000 members.

Friends of Libraries U.S.A. (FOLUSA, founded 1979) merged with the Association for Library Trustees and Advocates (ALTA) in 2009 to form ALA's United for Libraries, serving Trustees, Friends, and Foundations.
A 1987 FOLUSA study found Friends groups averaged 213 members and raised $9,408 per year for furniture, equipment, books, and programming.

The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation's U.S. Libraries initiative began in 1997 to connect public libraries to the internet, reaching library systems across all 50 states with computers, software, and training; the international Global Libraries program extended this to 30+ countries.
The Gates Foundation committed more than $1 billion cumulatively to library programs (US and global) before winding down Global Libraries ~2018.
The New York Public Library holds an endowment of ~$1.45 billion (2017), founded from the Astor, Lenox, and Tilden Foundations and Carnegie's $5.2 million grant for 65 branches.
The Andrew W. Mellon Foundation, with a ~$6.1 billion endowment and a $540 million annual grant budget (2024), is a leading funder of libraries, humanities, and scholarly communication.
The Carnegie Corporation of New York (founded 1911 with a $135 million endowment) holds a ~$4.1 billion endowment (2022) and continues Carnegie's knowledge-advancement mission.
ALA's United for Libraries coordinates the National Friends of Libraries Week (21st annual in 2026), Literary Landmark program (60+ sites by 2009), and statewide training in 12 states.
Alaska and Delaware are the only US states with no Carnegie libraries.
Indiana (165), California (142), and Illinois/New York/Ohio (106 each) had the most Carnegie public libraries by state.
Women's clubs led the establishment of 75-80% of libraries in communities across the country during Carnegie's era.
Under segregation, Carnegie funded separate libraries for African Americans in the South (e.g., Houston Colored Carnegie Library; Savannah, GA Carnegie Library opened 1914).
Adopt-a-Book and similar sponsor-a-book programs operate at many libraries (e.g., Smithsonian Libraries) and are promoted by ALA United for Libraries.
philanthropy.source_notes: Primary sources retrieved Aug 2026 and cached in data/_cache/ with prefix 'philanthropy_': Wikipedia REST API/HTML articles (Carnegie library; List of Carnegie libraries in the United States; Carnegie Corporation of New York; Andrew W. Mellon Foundation; Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation; Friends of Libraries; New York Public Library; Chicago Public Library; Boston Public Library; San Francisco Public Library; Smithsonian Libraries); Carnegie Corporation of New York official history page (carnegie.org/about/our-history); ALA United for Libraries official pages (ala.org/united); Wayback Machine archived Gates Foundation Global Libraries pages (2012 snapshot). Carnegie by-state figures were programmatically parsed from the Wikipedia 'List of Carnegie libraries in the United States' detail table (50 states/territories with Carnegie libraries; Alaska and Delaware excluded as having none). Dollar figures for Carnegie grants are historical nominal dollars (1883-1929); modern equivalents noted where Wikipedia provided them. The Gates Foundation Global Libraries total committed figure (>$1 billion) is a widely-reported estimate; the foundation's current website is JavaScript-rendered and does not expose a single published total on static HTML, so the figure is marked as an estimate. Total annual private giving to US libraries is not published as a single authoritative number by IMLS, ALA, or Candid; private/donated revenue is reported inconsistently across ~9,200 public library systems and is not aggregated nationally. ALA United for Libraries subpages (Adopt-a-Book, funding toolkits) are JavaScript-rendered and returned only navigation chrome via static fetch, so Adopt-a-Book details are drawn from the Smithsonian Libraries article and United for Libraries main-page program listings.

circulation.source: IMLS Public Libraries Survey FY2024, compiled via ALA State of America's Libraries data
circulation.data_year: FY2022 (reported in ALA 2024 report as latest finalized PLS data)
circulation.source_notes: Total circulation includes physical and electronic materials. Electronic circulation (e-books, e-audiobooks) is a subset and may overlap with total_circulation depending on state reporting methodology. IMLS uses negative sentinels (-1, -3, -40) for suppressed/unreported values, normalized to 0. Registered borrowers = registered library card holders as reported by each state. Per-capita figures computed by dividing by population served (minimum 1,000). Children's circulation percentage only computed for states with >100,000 total circulation to avoid small-number noise.
key_facts: Americans checked out 1.71 billion items from public libraries in FY2022 - roughly 5.2 items per person in the United States.
155 million Americans hold library cards - about 45% of the population served by public libraries.
Electronic (e-book/e-audio) circulation reached 316 million, about 18.5% of total circulation - up from near-zero two decades ago.
Children's materials account for 36.9% of circulation (630M items), making children the single largest user demographic by material type.
Americans made 869 million visits to public libraries - 2.5 visits per capita.
Libraries hosted 5.1 million programs attended by 105 million people.
101 million people used public library computers/internet in FY2022.
Public library collections hold 639 million book volumes nationally.

metadata.title: US Public Library Card Registration & Circulation Summary

national_stats.total_cardholders_note: Sum of registered_borrowers across all reporting states/territories (IMLS PLS FY2024, 55 jurisdictions reporting the field). The ALA widely cites ~166-170M Americans with library cards as an advocacy estimate counting active and household cards, which exceeds the raw registered-borrower count.
national_stats.pct_population_note: Registered borrowers / legal service area population served (PLS). The raw IMLS registered-borrower count yields ~45%; the ALA advocacy figure implies ~50%+ of the total US population.
national_stats.total_circulation_note: Official IMLS PLS FY2024 national total (sum of total_circulation across reporting jurisdictions; states that suppressed the field are excluded). Pre-pandemic FY2019 was ~2.19B.
national_stats.total_circulation_best_estimate_note: Adds physical-only circulation as a lower-bound estimate for the 4 states (FL, IA, MA, OR) that suppressed total_circulation; electronic circulation for those states is unknown.
national_stats.digital_vs_physical_note: Digital share computed from the 49 jurisdictions reporting BOTH physical and electronic circulation (electronic = ebooks + e-audio + e-video).
national_stats.source: IMLS Public Libraries Survey (PLS) FY2024 (aggregated in data/_cache/ala_state_data.json); ALA State of America's Libraries Report 2024 for the cardholder advocacy estimate.

trends.value: COVID-19 pandemic: physical visits collapsed (~-42%) while digital/e-circulation surged; libraries shifted to curbside pickup and expanded digital collections. FY2021 omitted due to IMLS data-structure changes.
E-circulation (ebooks, e-audio, e-video) stabilized near ~28% of circulation; physical circulation remains the majority but its share has declined from pre-pandemic levels.

demographics.source: Pew Research Center, Internet & American Life Project — Library Services Survey (n=6,224, ages 16+, July 18-Sept 30, 2013)
demographics.report: How Americans Value Public Libraries in Their Communities (Jan 2014)
demographics.cardholder_profile: Card holders are more likely to be female, white, under age 65, and suburban/urban residents, and to have higher levels of education or live in higher-income households.

age_groups.note: Pew 2013 — % who have EVER visited a public library/bookmobile in person (% visited in past 12 months)

income_levels.note: Pew 2013, adults 18+ — % ever visited / % visited past 12 months

education_levels.note: Pew 2013, adults 18+ — % ever visited / % visited past 12 months

digital_vs_physical.trend: Digital/electronic circulation (ebooks, downloadable audio/video) grew rapidly 2010-2020 and surged during COVID-19, stabilizing near ~28% of circulation in FY2024. Physical circulation remains the majority (~72%) but its share has declined from pre-pandemic levels as digital borrowing normalizes.
digital_vs_physical.breakdown_note: Electronic circulation = ebooks + e-audio + e-video downloads/streams reported to IMLS PLS; does not include in-house database use or online program views. Share computed across the 49 jurisdictions reporting both physical and electronic circulation.
digital_vs_physical.childrens_note: Children's materials (picture books, juvenile fiction/nonfiction, YA) account for ~37% of total circulation — the single largest content category — reflecting libraries' central role in early literacy and family services.

key_facts: Approximately 155 million Americans were registered library borrowers in FY2024 (IMLS PLS); the ALA estimates ~166-170 million Americans have library cards when counting active and household cards.

US public libraries circulated 1.71 billion items in FY2024 (official IMLS total; ~1.86B including best estimates for states that suppressed the field) — about 4.97 items per person in the population served.
Children's materials make up ~37% of all circulation, the single largest content category.
Digital/electronic circulation is ~28% of circulation; physical materials remain ~72%.
September is Library Card Sign-Up Month, an ALA national campaign launched in 1987 to encourage card enrollment, timed with the start of the school year.
Pew Research (2013) found 61% of Americans age 16+ have a library card (down from 63% in 2012); cardholders skew female, white, under 65, suburban/urban, higher-education, and higher-income.
86% of Americans age 16+ have used a public library at some point (in person or via website); 54% used one in the past 12 months (Pew 2013).
Circulation peaked around FY2019 (~2.19B items), fell ~25% in FY2020 during COVID-19, rebounded to ~1.96B by FY2023, then eased to ~1.71B in FY2024 as digital borrowing normalized.
Physical library visits collapsed ~42% in FY2020 (from ~1.25B to ~732M) during pandemic closures and have only partially recovered (~869M in FY2024).
Registration rates vary widely by state (roughly 30%-70% of the served population), reflecting differences in data reporting, card-expiration policies, and community outreach.
library_cards.source_notes: PRIMARY DATA: IMLS Public Libraries Survey (PLS) FY2024 — registered_borrowers, total_circulation, physical_circulation, electronic_circulation, children_circulation, population_served — aggregated by state/territory in data/_cache/ala_state_data.json (sourced from pls_fy2024_state_summary.json). 56 reporting jurisdictions (50 states + DC + territories). IMLS uses sentinel codes (e.g. -79) for suppressed/missing values; 4 states (FL, IA, MA, OR) suppressed total_circulation. The official national total (1.705B) excludes them; a best-estimate total (1.862B) adds their physical circulation as a lower bound (electronic unknown). Historical circulation FY2019-FY2024 from data/_cache/pls_historical_trends.json (FY2021 omitted due to IMLS data-structure changes). NATIONAL CARDHOLDER ESTIMATE: The American Library Association (ALA) 'Quotable Facts About America's Libraries' and advocacy materials broadly cite ~166-170M Americans with library cards; this counts active and household cards and exceeds the raw IMLS registered-borrower sum (~155M), partly because not all jurisdictions report the field and the ALA figure includes household-level estimates. DEMOGRAPHICS: Pew Research Center Internet & American Life Project, Library Services Survey (n=6,224, ages 16+, July 18-Sept 30, 2013), report 'How Americans Value Public Libraries in Their Communities' (Jan 2014); retrieved via an Internet Archive Wayback snapshot of the original Pew PDF (Pew's current site restructured the legacy /internet/ URLs to 404). Card-ownership rate: 61% (vs 63% in Nov 2012). LIBRARY CARD SIGN-UP MONTH: ALA national campaign, observed each September since 1987. LIMITATIONS: ALA.org and IMLS.gov public web pages were largely inaccessible from this environment (404s/timeouts following ALA's 2024 site restructuring), so the ALA cardholder estimate and Sign-Up Month facts are cited as established ALA figures corroborated by Wikipedia citations rather than freshly fetched. All quantitative cardholder/circulation/per-capita figures derive from the locally cached IMLS PLS FY2024 raw data, the authoritative government source.
