tribal_libraries.source_notes: This summary was compiled on 2026-08-14 from IMLS grant award data extracted from a cached dataset (FY1998-FY2013) and from Wikipedia articles that cite primary sources (ATALM, IMLS, AIHEC, AILA, ALA, FCC, and academic publications). All dollar figures and counts derived from the IMLS dataset are factual aggregates of that dataset; all other figures are attributed to their cited sources. Where the live IMLS and ATALM websites were unreachable during research (HTTP 404 or timeout), the Wikipedia articles citing those organizations' primary documents were used. Figures flagged as estimates reflect the absence of a single authoritative census of tribal libraries.

academic_stats.title: U.S. Academic Libraries — Statistics Summary
academic_stats.data_year_primary: 2022-23 (IPEDS AL Survey); 2012 (NCES ALS, last year of full service metrics); ARL FY2022
academic_stats.description: Comprehensive statistics on degree-granting academic (college/university) libraries in the United States, drawn from the NCES Academic Library Survey (ALS, 2000-2012), the IPEDS Academic Library (AL) component (2014-present), the Association of Research Libraries (ARL) Statistics, and Wikipedia articles citing primary sources. Holdings, expenditure, staffing, ILL, and Carnegie-class breakdown figures are computed directly from the NCES/IPEDS public-use microdata files; ARL aggregate figures come from the ARL organization and its Wikipedia article.

total_count.survey_universe_note: NCES states it 'collects data biennially from about 3,700 degree-granting postsecondary institutions' via the Academic Library survey (nces.ed.gov/surveys/libraries/academic.asp). This is the population of U.S. academic libraries as defined by NCES — the library associated with a degree-granting institution of higher education.
total_count.institutions_in_ipeds_universe_note: The broader IPEDS institutional universe (academic_institution_profiles.csv, IPEDS 2023) contains 6,163 degree-granting institutions, but many very small or special-focus institutions are out-of-scope for the library survey or do not report library data.
total_count.respondents_2022_23_note: Rows in the IPEDS AL 2022-23 revised data file (al2022_rv.csv). Of these, 2,862 reported full expenditure data; 3,438 reported staffing; 3,539 reported physical volume counts. Non-response on individual items is common.
total_count.respondents_2012_als_note: The standalone NCES Academic Library Survey 2012 (ALS_2012) collected data from 4,261 institutions — the peak count before the survey was folded into IPEDS in 2014.
total_count.trend_note: The respondent count has declined modestly since 2012 (4,261 -> 3,695 in 2023), reflecting institutional closures, consolidations, and the contraction of the U.S. higher-education sector (especially among small private and for-profit colleges).
total_count.source: NCES Library Statistics Program — Academic Libraries overview (data/_cache/academic_nces_overview.html); IPEDS AL 2022-23 revised data file (data/_cache/ipeds_al_historical/2022-23/al2022_rv.csv); NCES ALS 2012 final data file (data/_cache/als2012_tmp/).

by_carnegie_class.note: Includes both 'Very High Research Activity' (R1, 108 institutions) and 'High Research Activity' (R2, 98) plus Doctoral/Professional Universities (83). These research universities account for 61.5% of all U.S. academic library expenditures despite being only ~10% of respondent libraries.
Community and two-year colleges. Largest group of respondents by count, but small average budgets (~$797K).
Faith-related, health-professions, arts/music/design, law, medical, business, and technical schools.
Tribally Controlled Colleges and Universities (TCUs). 33 TCUs exist in the IPEDS universe; 23 reported library data in 2022-23.
Institutions without a current Carnegie classification (Code -2), typically newer, very small, or newly-classified entities.

academic_stats.by_carnegie_class_note: Aggregates computed by joining the IPEDS AL 2022-23 revised file to the institutional profile file (academic_institution_profiles.csv) on UNITID and grouping by the 2022 Carnegie Classification broad category. Sums are over the 2,862 institutions that reported full expenditure data. See data/_cache/academic_ipeds_al_2022_23_aggregates.json for the full breakdown including the complete Carnegie detail list (108 R1, 98 R2, etc.).

total_holdings.physical_volumes_2022_23_note: Sum of LPBOOKS across 3,539 reporting institutions in IPEDS AL 2022-23. IPEDS 'physical books' is a narrower count than the legacy ALS/ARL 'total volumes held' metric (which historically included microforms, audio, and government documents). For comparison, the NCES ALS 2012 reported 1,102,789,126 physical book volumes HELD (COLBKSH) across 4,261 institutions, plus 1,045,866,960 microform units and 123,325,126 audio units held.
total_holdings.ebooks_2022_23_note: Sum of LEBOOKS across 3,741 reporting institutions. E-book holdings now exceed physical book volumes more than 2:1 in the aggregate, reflecting site-licensed e-book packages (e.g., EBSCO, JSTOR, ProQuest Ebook Central).
total_holdings.electronic_serial_titles_note: Electronic serial titles outnumber physical serial titles ~66:1 (98.5% of serial titles are electronic), reflecting the near-complete migration of journal collections to e-formats. Note: IPEDS counts serial TITLES, not subscriptions; one aggregator package can contribute hundreds of thousands of title counts.
total_holdings.total_collection_items_note: Sum of LTCLLCT (physical + electronic collection totals). This very large figure reflects the inclusion of site-licensed e-serial title counts and e-book package counts.
total_holdings.source: IPEDS AL 2022-23 revised data file (data/_cache/ipeds_al_historical/2022-23/al2022_rv.csv); NCES ALS 2012 final data file (data/_cache/als2012_tmp/ALS_2012_imp_suppr_20130724.txt); aggregates in data/_cache/academic_ipeds_al_2022_23_aggregates.json and data/_cache/academic_als_2012_aggregates.json.

arl.name: Association of Research Libraries (ARL)
arl.member_count_note: ARL's Wikipedia infobox (edited July 2026) lists 125 members. Membership includes research libraries in the U.S. AND Canada (e.g., University of Toronto, McGill, University of British Columbia), plus the Library of Congress, National Agricultural Library, National Library of Medicine, New York Public Library, Boston Public Library, and the Smithsonian Institution — so the count of U.S. academic-library members is somewhat lower than 125.
arl.annual_spending_note: Per ARL's own description: member libraries 'make up a large portion of the academic and research library marketplace, spending approximately $4.5 billion every year on information resources.' (Wikipedia/Association of Research Libraries, citing arl.org).
arl.total_volumes_note: ARL libraries collectively hold the largest share of U.S. academic library print volumes. Based on the IPEDS AL 2022-23 data, the 289 Doctoral University respondents alone reported 434.4M physical volumes; ARL-member research libraries (a subset weighted toward the very largest doctoral institutions) are estimated to hold on the order of 500M+ volumes collectively. Historically ARL reported aggregate 'total volumes held' exceeding 500 million in the 2000s-2010s.
arl.statistics_program: ARL Statistics — published annually since 1963; the gold-standard descriptive statistical series for North American research libraries. Covers volumes held & added, serials, expenditures (by category), staffing, salaries (ARL Annual Salary Survey), interlibrary loan, and preservation. ARL also publishes ARL Academic Health Sciences Library Statistics, ARL Academic Law Library Statistics, ClimateQUAL, LibQUAL+, and the Research Library Impact Framework.
arl.affiliations: ARL co-founded the Coalition for Networked Information (CNI) with EDUCAUSE in 1990. ARL is a member of the Library Copyright Alliance (with ALA and ACRL).

arl_acrl_relationship.arl_status: ARL remains an independent nonprofit membership organization as of 2026.
arl_acrl_relationship.acrl_status: The Association of College and Research Libraries (ACRL) is a division of the American Library Association (ALA). ACRL's standalone Wikipedia article has been merged into the ALA article (Wikipedia redirect confirmed via the MediaWiki API in August 2026).
arl_acrl_relationship.merger_claim_note: The task brief referenced an 'ARL merged into ACRL around 2022-2024.' Based on sources reviewed in August 2026, ARL has NOT merged into ACRL — ARL continues to operate as an independent organization with its own executive director (Andrew K. Pace, since 2024) and 125 members. ALA has, however, been restructuring its OWN divisions: in 2019-2020 ALA consolidated three divisions (ALCTS, LITA, LLAMA) into 'Core: Leadership, Infrastructure, Futures,' and on August 31, 2026 the Young Adult Library Services Association (YALSA) was dissolved and reunified with ALSC. ACRL itself remains one of ALA's eight membership divisions. The ARL/ACRL/ALA relationship is one of affiliation (joint Library Copyright Alliance) rather than merger.
arl_acrl_relationship.source: Wikipedia 'Association of Research Libraries' (data/_cache/ill_wiki_arl.txt, edited 2026-07-27); Wikipedia 'American Library Association' incl. ACRL section (data/_cache/academic_wiki_acrl2.html); Wikipedia API redirect check for ACRL -> ALA.

arl.executive_director_2024: Andrew K. Pace (since 2024; predecessor Mary Lee Kennedy 2018-2024)
arl.source: Wikipedia 'Association of Research Libraries' (data/_cache/ill_wiki_arl.html, data/_cache/ill_wiki_arl.txt); ARL website (arl.org).

expenditures.total_usd_2022_23_note: Sum of LEXPTOT across 2,862 reporting institutions in IPEDS AL 2022-23. This is total library expenditures (materials + salaries + other operating). It is the figure most comparable to the 'about $3-4 billion' historical estimate, but the post-2014 IPEDS totals run higher (~$8B) because the survey scope and accounting basis changed when the survey moved from NCES to IPEDS.
expenditures.median_note: ARL publishes median (not mean) library expenditures for its members. ARL member library expenditures are far higher than the sector median: large research universities spend tens of millions annually (Harvard, Yale, Michigan, etc.), while the typical small college library spends well under $1M. The ARL Annual Salary Survey and ARL Statistics provide the median figures for member libraries.

trend.note: Survey transferred from NCES to IPEDS; accounting basis changed, so 2014+ figures are not strictly comparable to 2012 and earlier.

expenditures.trend_note: Figures for 2000-2012 are from the NCES Academic Library Survey (ALS) totals in als_trends_national.csv; 2014-2023 are from the IPEDS AL component. The 2014 discontinuity reflects a change in survey administration and accounting (e.g., inclusion of fringe benefits and reclassification of some cost lines), NOT a real one-year jump of ~$1.8B. In nominal dollars, total reported academic library spending rose ~73% from 2000 to 2023.
expenditures.source: NCES ALS / IPEDS AL national trends (data/als_trends_national.csv; data/_cache/academic_als_ipeds_national_trend.json); IPEDS AL 2022-23 revised microdata (data/_cache/ipeds_al_historical/2022-23/al2022_rv.csv); ARL spending figure from Wikipedia 'Association of Research Libraries' citing arl.org.

staffing.total_fte_2022_23_note: Sum of LSTOTAL across 3,438 reporting institutions in IPEDS AL 2022-23.

trend.note: 2012 was the last ALS year; professional librarians (STLIBPRO) totaled 35,088 FTE across 4,261 institutions.
IPEDS AL; spike may reflect pandemic-year reporting and temporary student staff.

staffing.trend_note: Total library staff FTE peaked around 2008-2012 (27,000+ across ~4,000 respondents) and has declined to ~24,450 across ~3,440 respondents in 2023. The decline reflects both reduced staffing per library (budget pressure, automation, e-resource shifts reducing technical-services work) and the smaller respondent pool. Professional librarian FTE specifically fell from 35,088 (ALS 2012) to 24,488 (IPEDS 2022-23) — a ~30% drop — though definitions differ between the two surveys.
staffing.declining_professional_librarians_note: As budgets tighten and collections shift to licensed e-resources (which require less local technical processing than print), many academic libraries have reduced professional librarian lines and shifted toward paraprofessional and student staffing. The ALS 2012 found 35,088 professional librarian FTE (STLIBPRO) plus 18,382 student assistant FTE among 4,261 institutions.
staffing.source: NCES ALS / IPEDS AL national trends (data/als_trends_national.csv); IPEDS AL 2022-23 revised microdata; ALS 2012 microdata (data/_cache/academic_als_2012_aggregates.json).

largest_by_volumes.note: Harvard Library is the largest strictly academic library in the world, with over 20 million volumes, 400 million manuscripts, 10 million photographs, and 1 million maps (Wikipedia/Academic library).

largest_by_volumes.institution: Columbia University in the City of New York
The University of Texas at Austin

largest_by_volumes.note: UCLA's IPEDS 2022-23 figure (14.3M) is the highest in the file; the large jump from 2012 reflects the UC system's consolidated reporting and inclusion of additional collection categories.

academic_stats.largest_by_volumes_note: The 2012 figures are 'total volumes HELD' (COLBKSH) from the NCES Academic Library Survey 2012, the last year NCES collected the comprehensive volumes-held metric and the most directly comparable to ARL 'total volumes held.' The 2022-23 figures are 'physical books' (LPBOOKS) from IPEDS, a NARROWER metric that excludes microforms, audio, and some government-document categories historically counted in 'volumes held' — which is why several institutions show LOWER numbers in 2022-23 than 2012 despite collection growth. Harvard is consistently ranked the largest U.S. academic library. Wikipedia (Academic library) reports Harvard at 'over 20 million volumes' and notes the University of California system operates the largest academic library SYSTEM in the world, managing about 41 million volumes across 100 libraries on ten campuses. ALS 2012 also surfaced an anomalous community college (Tarrant County College District, 7.83M) reflecting that institution's broad reporting of its holdings.
academic_stats.largest_by_volumes_source: NCES ALS 2012 microdata (data/_cache/academic_als_2012_aggregates.json); IPEDS AL 2022-23 revised microdata joined to academic_institution_profiles.csv (data/_cache/academic_ipeds_al_2022_23_aggregates.json); Wikipedia 'Academic library' (data/_cache/academic_wiki_academic_library.html).

digital_transition.eresource_spending_share_note: The IPEDS AL survey's materials-expenditure line for 'current serial subscriptions' (LEXMSCS, $2.55B = 78.9% of materials spending) captures the dominance of ongoing e-serial/journal subscriptions — the bulk of which are now electronic. ARL and ACRL surveys have long shown that at major research universities, e-resource spending exceeds 70% of the materials budget, and at some institutions exceeds 80%. The 'big deal' journal packages from major publishers (Elsevier, Wiley, Springer Nature, Taylor & Francis, SAGE) and database licenses (EBSCO, JSTOR, ProQuest, Scopus, Web of Science) drive this spending.
digital_transition.decline_of_print_serials: Print journal subscriptions have collapsed as libraries cancelled print in favor of electronic access. The 98.5% e-share of serial TITLES (1.54B electronic vs 23.2M physical) reflects both genuine e-migration and the counting effect of aggregator packages that report vast title counts.
digital_transition.open_access_rise: Open access (OA) publishing and OA repositories have grown sharply since the early 2000s, driven by funder mandates (NIH Public Access Policy 2008, OSTP memos 2013/2022), the growth of OA publishers (PLOS, BMC, Frontiers), and 'transformative agreements' (read-and-publish deals) between libraries/consortia and publishers. ARL's Toward an Open Monograph Ecosystem (TOME) initiative and SPARC (Scholarly Publishing and Academic Resources Coalition, founded by ARL in 1998) advance open scholarship. Preprint servers (arXiv, bioRxiv, SSRN) and institutional repositories further reduce reliance on licensed serials.
digital_transition.source: IPEDS AL 2022-23 revised microdata (data/_cache/ipeds_al_historical/2022-23/al2022_rv.csv); ARL priorities page (arl.org); Wikipedia 'Association of Research Libraries'.

reference_trend.note: Reference transactions and gate counts were DROPPED from the IPEDS AL survey beginning 2014. The IPEDS AL component collects only expenditures, staffing, collections, and ILL — NOT reference transactions, circulation, gate counts, or presentations. As a result, no national academic-library reference statistics are collected after 2012.

academic_stats.reference_trend_note: The NCES Academic Library Survey 2012 was the LAST year national reference-transaction, gate-count, and presentation data were collected for U.S. academic libraries. In 2012, the 4,261 reporting institutions recorded 29,308,016 total service transactions (TOTSERIN, a category that included reference), 541,940 presentations (PRESEN) attended by 10,217,555 people, and a gate count of 22,614,482 (GATECT, though this field's national coverage was partial). Academic-library reference transactions had been declining for years before 2012 as discovery layers (Summon, Primo, EDS), Google, and chat/async reference displaced in-person desk transactions. ALA/RUSA and ACRL documented this decline through the 2000s. The disappearance of the metric post-2012 means current national reference trends cannot be tracked from federal data; individual library LibQUAL+ and local assessments fill some of the gap.
academic_stats.reference_trend_source: NCES ALS 2012 microdata (data/_cache/academic_als_2012_aggregates.json); NCES ALS 2012 SAS layout (data/_cache/als2012_sas_layout.txt); NCES survey overview (data/_cache/academic_nces_overview.html).

interlibrary_loan.total_ill_transactions_note_2022_23: IPEDS AL 2022-23 reports 5,292,050 returnable (physical loans) and 4,753,857 non-returnable (digital copies) items PROVIDED (lent) by reporting libraries. IPEDS records only lending-provided, not borrowing-received.
interlibrary_loan.trend_note: ILL activity roughly halved between 2012 and 2022-23 (20.3M total -> 10.0M total), reflecting (a) expanded e-resource licensing reducing need for article ILL, (b) document delivery via ILLiad/RAPIDILL/Tipasa, and (c) the rise of shared print repositories and collective-collection agreements. Academic libraries remain the MAJOR participants in U.S. ILL: research universities are net lenders, while smaller colleges and public libraries are net borrowers. OCLC's WorldShare ILL, ILLiad, and Tipasa are the dominant platforms; the Center for Research Libraries (CRL) and the Committee on Institutional Cooperation (CIC, now the Big Ten Academic Alliance) operate shared-collection programs.
interlibrary_loan.source: IPEDS AL 2022-23 revised microdata (LILLDPR, LILLDRC); NCES ALS 2012 microdata (ILPTOT, ILRTOT); complements data/ill_summary.json.

space_and_hours.weekly_hours_note: Mean weekly hours open across 4,261 reporting academic libraries in ALS 2012. Ranges from part-time hours at small colleges to 168 hours (24/7) at major research universities.
space_and_hours.gate_count_note: Sum of GATECT in ALS 2012; reporting was partial (many institutions did not report gate counts, so the true national gate count is higher). Gate counting is itself declining as libraries replace turnstiles with card-swipe and Wi-Fi-based occupancy systems.
space_and_hours.library_as_place_movement: Since the early 2000s, academic libraries have repositioned themselves as collaborative learning spaces — the 'library as place' movement. Major renovations have converted stack space into group study rooms, silent floors, makerspaces, digital scholarship centers, cafes, and 24/7 study areas. The Society for College and University Planning (SCUP) and ACRL have documented this shift. Enrollment growth and the demand for student space drove large library building/renovation projects in the 2000s-2010s.
space_and_hours.hours_trend_24_7: Many large research universities extended hours to 24/7 (or near-24/7) during the semester, often through a combination of staffed service hours and unstaffed 'after hours' study access. The COVID-19 pandemic (2020-21) temporarily reduced or closed hours at most academic libraries; recovery to pre-pandemic hours was uneven and some libraries permanently reduced overnight hours.
space_and_hours.study_space_expansion: Post-pandemic, many academic libraries expanded reservable study rooms, added individual focus pods, and increased seating density to support both collaborative and quiet study. Information commons and learning commons models (pioneered by institutions like the University of Southern California's Leavey Library in the 1990s) are now standard.
space_and_hours.source: NCES ALS 2012 microdata (HOURS, GATECT fields); Wikipedia 'Academic library' (data/_cache/academic_wiki_academic_library.html); ACRL/SCUP literature on library as place.

key_facts: There are approximately 3,700 degree-granting academic libraries in the United States, per the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES), which surveys them biennially. The IPEDS AL 2022-23 data file contains 3,741 institutions, of which 2,862 reported full expenditure data. (NCES, nces.ed.gov/surveys/libraries/academic.asp)

U.S. academic libraries collectively reported $8.20 billion in total expenditures in 2022-23 (IPEDS AL), of which $3.23 billion (39%) was for materials (books, serials, e-resources), $3.42 billion (42%) for salaries and wages, $814 million for fringe benefits, and $740 million for other operating costs. (IPEDS AL 2022-23 revised microdata)

The Association of Research Libraries (ARL), founded in 1932, has 125 member research libraries in the U.S. and Canada that collectively spend approximately $4.5 billion per year on information resources — a large share of the entire academic library marketplace. ARL Statistics, published since 1963, is the gold-standard descriptive series for research libraries. (Wikipedia/Association of Research Libraries citing arl.org)

Harvard Library is the largest strictly academic library in the world, holding over 20 million volumes, 400 million manuscripts, 10 million photographs, and 1 million maps. The University of California system operates the largest academic library SYSTEM in the world, managing about 41 million volumes across 100 libraries on ten campuses. (Wikipedia/Academic library)

By NCES ALS 2012 volumes-held counts, the largest U.S. academic libraries were Harvard (17.2M), Yale (13.5M), University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (12.9M), UC Berkeley (11.5M), University of Michigan (11.5M), University of Chicago (11.4M), Columbia (11.3M), UT Austin (10.2M), UCLA (10.0M), and Indiana University (9.3M). (NCES ALS 2012 microdata)

Electronic serial titles now outnumber physical serial titles by roughly 66-to-1 (1.54 billion electronic vs 23.2 million physical in IPEDS 2022-23), and current serial subscriptions account for 78.9% of academic library materials spending — illustrating the near-complete migration of journal collections to electronic formats and the budget dominance of 'big deal' publisher packages and database licenses. (IPEDS AL 2022-23)

The NCES Academic Library Survey 2012 was the LAST year national reference-transaction, gate-count, and presentation data were collected. In 2012, reporting libraries recorded 29.3 million service transactions, 541,940 presentations attended by 10.2 million people, and a gate count of 22.6 million. These service metrics were dropped when the survey moved to IPEDS in 2014, so current national reference trends cannot be tracked from federal data. (NCES ALS 2012)

Total library staff FTE in reporting academic libraries declined from a pre-recession peak of ~27,164 (2008) to ~24,450 (2023), and professional librarian FTE fell from 35,088 (ALS 2012) to 24,488 (IPEDS 2022-23) — a ~30% drop — as budgets tightened, e-resources reduced local technical processing, and institutions shifted toward paraprofessional and student staffing. (NCES ALS / IPEDS AL)

Interlibrary loan activity in academic libraries roughly halved between 2012 and 2022-23 (from 20.3M to 10.0M total lending transactions), reflecting expanded e-resource licensing, document-delivery automation (ILLiad, RAPIDILL, Tipasa), and shared-print agreements — though academic libraries remain the major participants in U.S. ILL, with research universities as net lenders. (NCES ALS 2012 / IPEDS AL 2022-23)

Doctoral/Research Universities (289 respondents in 2022-23) account for 61.5% of all U.S. academic library expenditures ($5.04B of $8.20B) and 59% of physical volumes (434M of 705M), despite representing only ~10% of reporting libraries — a dramatic concentration of resources at research universities versus the 846 Associate's (community) college libraries which collectively spend $675M. (IPEDS AL 2022-23)

ARL has NOT merged into ACRL. As of 2026 ARL remains an independent 125-member organization (executive director Andrew K. Pace); ACRL is a division of the American Library Association. The two organizations are affiliated through the Library Copyright Alliance. ALA has, however, restructured its own divisions — consolidating ALCTS/LITA/LLAMA into 'Core' (2019-20) and dissolving YALSA (reunified with ALSC) on August 31, 2026. (Wikipedia/Association of Research Libraries, Wikipedia/American Library Association)

The mean weekly hours of operation across reporting academic libraries was 69.3 in 2012 (ALS); large research universities commonly operate 24/7 during the academic term. The 'library as place' movement since the 2000s has driven conversion of stack space into group study rooms, learning commons, makerspaces, and digital scholarship centers. (NCES ALS 2012; ACRL/SCUP literature)
academic_stats.source_notes: PRIMARY MICRODATA (computed by this project): (1) IPEDS Academic Library (AL) Survey 2022-23 revised data file, NCES — data/_cache/ipeds_al_historical/2022-23/al2022_rv.csv — aggregates in data/_cache/academic_ipeds_al_2022_23_aggregates.json. This is the current federal academic-library survey, administered through IPEDS since 2014 (previously the standalone NCES Academic Library Survey, ALS). (2) NCES Academic Library Survey 2012 final data file (ALS_2012_imp_suppr_20130724.txt) + SAS layout (als2012_sas_layout.txt) — data/_cache/als2012_tmp/ — aggregates in data/_cache/academic_als_2012_aggregates.json. 2012 was the last year of the standalone ALS and the last year reference/gate/presentation/service-transaction metrics were collected. (3) NCES ALS / IPEDS AL national trend table, data/als_trends_national.csv — also cached as data/_cache/academic_als_ipeds_national_trend.json. (4) Institutional profile/Carnegie classification file, data/academic_institution_profiles.csv (IPEDS 2023), used to join UNITID -> institution name and Carnegie class. SECONDARY SOURCES (for context, ARL aggregates, and largest-library rankings): NCES Library Statistics Program — Academic Libraries overview page (data/_cache/academic_nces_overview.html); Wikipedia 'Academic library' (data/_cache/academic_wiki_academic_library.html, retrieved Aug 2026) citing Harvard Library and UC system figures; Wikipedia 'Association of Research Libraries' (data/_cache/ill_wiki_arl.txt, edited 2026-07-27) for the 125-member, $4.5B, 1932-founding, and statistics-program facts; Wikipedia 'American Library Association' incl. the ACRL division section (data/_cache/academic_wiki_acrl2.html) and the Wikipedia API redirect check confirming ACRL -> ALA. METHODOLOGY NOTES: IPEDS AL 'physical books' (LPBOOKS) is a narrower count than the legacy ALS/ARL 'total volumes held' (COLBKSH), so 2022-23 volume figures are not directly comparable to 2012 volumes-held figures (several institutions appear smaller in 2022-23 for this reason). The 2014 jump in total expenditures reflects a change in survey administration/accounting basis (NCES ALS -> IPEDS AL), not a real one-year increase. ARL publishes MEDIAN (not mean) figures for its member libraries; the ARL Statistics and ARL Annual Salary Survey are subscription/member products, so exact current-year ARL aggregates were not separately retrieved — the $4.5B figure is ARL's own published characterization of member spending. NCES and ARL live websites block some automated retrieval; data was obtained from the public-use microdata files and Wikipedia snapshots.

prison_libraries.topic: Prison libraries and library services to incarcerated people in the United States
prison_libraries.data_availability: There is NO single comprehensive national dataset on prison libraries. The Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS) collects prison and prisoner counts but does NOT systematically collect library-access data. The Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP) operates libraries in federal facilities but publishes no public inventory of them. State departments of corrections vary widely and most do not report library statistics. The figures below are compiled from BJS prison-population reports, ALA reports and standards, NIC topic resources, congressional press releases and bill text, Ithaka S+R research, and journalism. Where a number is an estimate or derived figure, it is flagged as such.

prison_counts.facility_census_note: The Census of State and Federal Adult Correctional Facilities is collected periodically (last published for 2019). BJS confirms it covers facility counts, programs, staff, and resources, but the 2019 detailed tables were not directly retrievable via the targeted URLs during this research. The widely cited figure from the 2019 census is approximately 1,677 state and federal correctional facilities. State prisons are operated by 50 state departments of corrections plus the Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP).
prison_counts.data_source: Bureau of Justice Statistics, Prisons Report Series: Preliminary Data Release, 2023 (NCJ 309396)

library_access.official_access_rate_note: No federal statistical agency publishes the percentage of U.S. prisons with library services. BJS collects prison and prisoner counts but not library-access data; BOP does not publish a public inventory of facility libraries; state departments of corrections report inconsistently. The figures below are qualitative findings and informal estimates, not official statistics.
library_access.ala_finding_on_service_quality: ALA (2025) reports that many so-called prison libraries are 'little more than a few dusty shelves, often not managed by trained library workers.' Some prisons have libraries 'worthy of the name,' but many others have 'only minimal or nonexistent services,' meaning many incarcerated people have 'no real access to a meaningful library and the expertise of librarians.'
library_access.ithaka_finding_on_law_vs_recreational: Ithaka S+R (2024) found that in some facilities the law library is effectively the only library resource, because departments of corrections are generally obligated to provide legal-access resources, while recreational reading libraries are 'effectively non-existent.'
library_access.filter_estimate_basis: Using ALA's $13/capita adequate-funding benchmark against the $60M over six years, the Act might fund services at roughly 500 facilities - about one-third of state prisons. This is an informal journalist estimate, not an official projection.
library_access.prison_library_staffing_range: Ithaka S+R (2024): staffing ranges from a professional librarian to a correctional officer to incarcerated individuals themselves. Many prison libraries depend on donations and outside organizations (including public libraries) for books and resources.
library_access.training_gap: Ithaka S+R (2024): none of the interviewed librarians had received specific training in prison librarianship; it is usually treated as a 'special library' topic in library schools with few training opportunities.
library_access.covid_impact: Ithaka S+R (2024): during COVID-19 many prison libraries were closed completely or sectioned off for social distancing, and prison libraries were impacted the most when departments of corrections made budget and staffing cuts.

state_level_data.note: No comparable state-level dataset on prison library access exists. Each state department of corrections sets its own policies on library hours, budgets, staffing, and technology, and most do not report library statistics. BJS publishes state-level prisoner counts but not library-access figures. The examples below are documented programs found in the research, not a complete inventory.

key_statistics.pell_grant_context: The 1994 ban on federal Pell Grant eligibility for incarcerated people ended on July 1, 2023, restoring access to federal financial aid for higher education in prison programs - a parallel development to the expansion of prison library services.
key_statistics.recidivism_savings_ratio: ALA (2025): whatever a state invests in prison education programs is estimated to save roughly five times that amount in future incarceration costs.

legislation.context: The Prison Libraries Act is the first federal bill to establish and expand library services within state and territory correctional facilities. The original 2023 version (H.R. 2825) had 45 Democratic cosponsors but never advanced out of committee. It was revived in January 2026 as H.R. 7247 with a Senate companion (S. 4320). The ALA June 2025 report references the Act as 'a strong start for Congressional support and funding for prison libraries.'

limitations: No comprehensive national census of prison libraries exists. BJS collects prison and prisoner counts but not library-access data.
BOP facility library inventories are not published as a public machine-readable dataset.
State departments of corrections vary widely; most do not report library statistics, and figures are not comparable across states.

The percentage of prisons with library services cannot be stated precisely. The ALA reports that many prisons have 'only minimal or nonexistent' library services, and Ithaka S+R found that in some facilities the law library is effectively the only library resource because recreational reading libraries are 'effectively non-existent'. No single percentage figure is published by a statistical agency.

The ~1,677 state+federal correctional facility figure derives from the BJS 2019 Census of State and Federal Adult Correctional Facilities; a more recent facility census total was not directly retrievable during this research.
The 'about one-third of state prisons' funding estimate is an informal journalistic calculation, not an official projection.
BOP population statistics and congress.wiki bill pages are JavaScript-rendered; live numeric values could not be scraped as static HTML and rely on BJS-confirmed yearend figures.
