Collaborative licensing of electronic resources rose to prominence in the mid-1990s as libraries shifted from print-focused collection development to online databases and e-journals.
OCLC's resource sharing network is the largest in the world with 10,000+ libraries; its Express digital delivery program fills copy requests in an average of 10 hours.
Internet2 operates a 100 Gbit/s network backbone connecting over 60,000 US educational, research, government, and community anchor institutions including public libraries and museums.
The Digital Public Library of America aggregates 53M+ items from 46 partner hubs across 40 states and 8,700+ contributing institutions, and launched the Banned Book Club in July 2023.
Lyrasis, formed in 2009 from the merger of SOLINET and PALINET, has 1,000+ members and serves as the organizational home for open-source projects including DSpace, Fedora, ArchivesSpace, and VIVO.
NISO, founded in 1939 as the Z39 Committee, develops standards including Z39.50 (database access protocol), Dublin Core (Z39.85), OpenURL (Z39.88), SUSHI (Z39.93), and JATS (Z39.96).
OhioLINK serves more than 800,000 students, faculty, and staff at 88 institutions with 117 libraries in Ohio.
VIVA's 74 member institutions include all 39 state-assisted Virginia colleges and universities, 34 independent (private, nonprofit) institutions, and the Library of Virginia.
TexShare began in 1994 with 53 publicly supported academic and medical libraries and has since expanded by statute to include public libraries, community colleges, and clinical medicine libraries.

Amigos Library Services, founded in 1974 by 22 libraries to bring OCLC access to the southwest, merged with MLNC in 2012 to become the largest library network west of the Mississippi River, serving libraries across 22 states.

Many libraries commonly belong to multiple consortia, so aggregate membership counts across consortia overcount unique libraries; OCLC's nearly 30,000 member libraries represent the largest single consortial membership.
The California Digital Library's 2021 transformative agreement with Elsevier is a prominent US example of consortial open-access negotiation, converting paywalled content to open access.

digital_libraries_enhanced.title: Digital Libraries & E-Books: The Digital Reading Revolution
digital_libraries_enhanced.overview: The digital library revolution has transformed how Americans access books, research, and cultural heritage. Project Gutenberg (1971) was the first digital library, offering free e-books decades before the term existed. The Internet Archive (1996) pioneered web preservation and digital lending. Google Books (2004) set out to scan every book ever published. HathiTrust (2008) created a shared research repository of 18+ million volumes. OverDrive (2003) became the dominant e-book lending platform for public libraries. The Digital Public Library of America (2013) aggregates 50+ million items from 5,000+ institutions. Together, these digital libraries represent a fundamental shift in how knowledge is preserved, discovered, and shared.

digital_libraries.name: Project Gutenberg
digital_libraries.description: The world's first digital library. Founded at the University of Illinois, it offers 70,000+ free e-books, mostly public domain classics. Predates the Internet by decades.
digital_libraries.key_feature: Free public domain e-books in multiple formats

digital_libraries.name: Internet Archive
digital_libraries.description: Non-profit digital library offering free universal access to 41M+ texts, 14M+ videos, 15M+ audio recordings, and the Wayback Machine with 835B+ archived web pages. Operates controlled digital lending of scanned books.
digital_libraries.key_feature: Wayback Machine (835B web pages); controlled digital lending

digital_libraries.name: Open Library
digital_libraries.description: An Internet Archive project with the goal of creating 'one web page for every book ever published.' Contains 20M+ book records with a wiki interface for community contributions.
digital_libraries.key_feature: One web page for every book ever published; editable catalog

digital_libraries.name: Google Books
digital_libraries.description: Google's ambitious project to scan every book ever published. Has scanned 40M+ books from major research libraries. Full text searchable; public domain works fully viewable. Sparked the Authors Guild v. Google lawsuit (settled 2013).

digital_libraries.name: HathiTrust
digital_libraries.description: Collaborative digital repository of 18M+ digitized volumes contributed by research libraries. Provides full-text search and access for users with print disabilities. Member-governed, with 200+ partner institutions.
digital_libraries.key_feature: Shared digital repository; access for print-disabled users

digital_libraries.name: OverDrive / Libby
digital_libraries.description: The dominant e-book and audiobook lending platform for public libraries. Serves 92,000+ libraries and schools worldwide. In 2023, library patrons checked out 600M+ digital titles. The Libby app is the primary consumer interface.
digital_libraries.key_feature: E-book/audiobook lending for 92K+ libraries; Libby app

digital_libraries.name: Digital Public Library of America (DPLA)
digital_libraries.description: Aggregator of digital resources from libraries, archives, and museums across America. Free access to 50M+ items from 5,000+ partners through a single discovery platform. Hubs include state libraries, service hubs, and content hubs.
digital_libraries.key_feature: National digital aggregation; 50M items from 5K partners

digital_libraries.name: Google Scholar
digital_libraries.description: Free academic search engine indexing full-text scholarly literature across all formats. Contains 389M+ documents including peer-reviewed papers, theses, books, and preprints.

wayback_machine.description: The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine has been archiving web pages since 1996. It contains 835B+ archived web pages and is the world's largest web archive. It has become a critical tool for researchers, journalists, and anyone needing to access deleted or changed web content.

key_events.event: Internet Archive founded; begins archiving web pages
Archive-It service launched for institutions to create their own archives
835B+ web pages archived; ~600M pages added daily

timeline.event: Michael Hart founds Project Gutenberg at University of Illinois - the first digital library
Brewster Kahle founds the Internet Archive; begins archiving the web
Wayback Machine publicly launched, providing free access to archived web pages
OverDrive launches e-book lending platform for libraries
Google Books project announced; begins scanning books from major research libraries
Open Library project initiated by Internet Archive
HathiTrust founded as shared digital repository by CIC libraries
Authors Guild v. Google settles; Google Books ruled fair use. DPLA launches with 2.4M items
Internet Archive launches controlled digital lending
COVID-19 drives massive surge in e-book borrowing; OverDrive records 430M checkouts
OverDrive surpasses 600M annual checkouts; DPLA reaches 50M items
Internet Archive loses Hachette v. Internet Archive lawsuit over controlled digital lending

key_facts: Project Gutenberg (1971) is the world's oldest digital library, founded 20 years before the World Wide Web became public
The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine contains 835 billion+ archived web pages, growing by ~600 million pages daily
Google Books has scanned over 40 million books, making it the largest single digitization effort in history
HathiTrust holds 18+ million digitized volumes from research libraries and provides full-text search across the entire collection
OverDrive served 600+ million digital checkouts in 2023 through 92,000+ libraries and schools in 100+ countries
The DPLA aggregates 50+ million digital items from 5,000+ cultural heritage institutions through a single free platform
Open Library aims to create 'one web page for every book ever published' and currently has 20+ million book records
The Internet Archive's controlled digital lending program allows one user at a time to borrow scanned books, mirroring physical lending
The Authors Guild v. Google (2013) established that mass book digitization for search constitutes fair use
The Internet Archive lost the Hachette v. Internet Archive (2024) lawsuit, which challenged controlled digital lending of scanned books
OverDrive's Libby app has been downloaded 50+ million times and is the primary way Americans borrow library e-books
COVID-19 accelerated e-book borrowing dramatically: OverDrive checkouts jumped from 350M in 2019 to 430M in 2020

reading_habits.title: Reading Habits & Literacy in America
reading_habits.overview: Americans' reading habits have shifted dramatically in the digital age. According to the NEA's Survey of Public Participation in the Arts (SPPA 2022), 23% of American adults read literature (novels, short stories, poetry, or plays) in the previous 12 months. The Pew Research Center found that 54% of Americans used a public library in 2013, and Gallup reported Americans averaged 10.5 library visits per year in 2019. Despite concerns about declining reading, e-book and audiobook borrowing through libraries has surged, with 600+ million digital checkouts in 2023. The relationship between library access, literacy, and reading habits remains a critical area of research.

nea_sppa_2022.survey: Survey of Public Participation in the Arts (SPPA) 2022
key_findings: 23% of US adults read literature (novels, short stories, poetry, or plays) in the previous 12 months
Reading rates declined from 47% in 1982 to 43% in 2008 to 23% in 2022 (definition changed over time)
Women read literature at higher rates than men (30% vs 16%)
White adults had the highest literary reading rate at 26%, followed by Black adults at 22%
Adults aged 18-24 had the lowest literary reading rate at 14%
College-educated adults read literature at 35%, compared to 12% for those without high school diplomas
Literary reading correlates positively with household income and educational attainment

pew_findings.survey: Pew Research Center - How Americans Use Public Libraries
key_findings: 54% of Americans used a public library in the past 12 months (2013 Pew survey)
Women are more likely than men to use libraries (60% vs 48%)
Parents of minor children are heavy library users (71% used library in past year)
53% of library users visit to sit and read, study, or watch/listen to media
49% of library users visit to borrow print books
17% of library users borrow e-books or audio books
30% of Americans are 'library lovers' who use libraries and view them positively
Library users tend to be more active in their communities than non-users
94% of Americans say that having a public library improves the quality of life in a community
76% of Americans say libraries provide necessary services to people who need them

literacy_data.source: National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) PIAAC
literacy_data.description: The Program for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) measures adult literacy. 14% of US adults perform at below basic prose literacy levels, struggling with simple text comprehension. This has significant implications for library services.

key_facts: Only 23% of American adults read literature (novels, short stories, poetry, or plays) in 2022, per the NEA SPPA survey
54% of Americans used a public library in the past 12 months (Pew Research Center 2013)
Americans average 10.5 library visits per year (Gallup 2019)
14% of US adults perform at below basic prose literacy levels, struggling with simple text comprehension (NCES PIAAC)
Women read literature at nearly double the rate of men (30% vs 16%, NEA 2022)
College-educated adults read literature at 35% compared to 12% for those without high school diplomas
Audiobooks are the fastest-growing reading format, with 23% of Americans listening regularly
Print books remain the dominant format, with 65% of readers preferring physical books
Library users are more civically engaged than non-users, volunteering and attending community events at higher rates
94% of Americans believe having a public library improves community quality of life
States with the highest literacy rates (NH, MN, ND at 93-94%) correlate with strong public library systems
States with the lowest literacy rates (MS, LA at 72%) also tend to have fewer school librarians per student
Digital checkouts through libraries exceeded 600 million in 2023, showing strong demand for e-books and audiobooks
The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated digital reading but reduced in-person library visits, creating a permanent shift in usage patterns

slide_inequities.title: School Library Inequities: The SLIDE Project
slide_inequities.overview: The SLIDE (School Librarian Investigation: Decline in Education) project documents stark inequities in school library staffing across the United States. Their research reveals that approximately 3 million students in majority-nonwhite districts lack access to a school librarian, and that school librarian losses have fallen disproportionately on districts serving Black, Latino, and Native American students. The project combines NCES data with demographic analysis to expose how the 20% national decline in school librarians since 2010 has created a two-tier system where wealthier, whiter districts retain librarians while poorer, diverse districts lose them.
inequity_findings: 3 million students in majority-nonwhite school districts attend schools without a librarian
54% of students in majority-nonwhite districts lack access to a school librarian (vs 24% in majority-white districts)
Schools with higher percentages of Black, Latino, and Native American students are more likely to have lost librarians
Rural districts are particularly affected: 35% have no librarian at all
Districts with the most students in poverty have lost librarians at 2-3x the rate of affluent districts
The decline in school librarians accelerated after the Great Recession (2008) and has not recovered
25 states have lost 20% or more of their school librarians since 2010
The geographic distribution of librarian losses maps closely to patterns of educational inequality
key_facts: The SLIDE project found that 3 million students in majority-nonwhite districts lack access to a school librarian
54% of students in majority-nonwhite districts attend schools without librarians, compared to 24% in majority-white districts
California lost 46% of its school librarians between 2010 and 2019, the largest decline of any state
Michigan lost 36% and Florida lost 31% of school librarians in the same period
The decline in school librarians closely tracks patterns of racial and economic inequality in American education
Rural districts are especially hard-hit, with 35% having no librarian at all
The SLIDE project combines NCES SASS data with demographic analysis from the Common Core of Data
Schools that lost librarians often simultaneously lost other support staff, compounding the impact on students
Research consistently shows that the absence of school librarians correlates with lower reading scores
The Every Student Succeeds Act (2015) allows states to use federal funds for school library programs, but few do
The SLIDE project recommends targeted state and federal investment to restore librarian positions in high-need districts
Without intervention, the school librarian equity gap is likely to widen as pandemic-era budget pressures continue

library_innovation.title: Library Innovation & Future Trends
library_innovation.description: A comprehensive reference on library innovation and future trends, covering AI in libraries (chatbots, AI cataloging, AI-powered discovery, ChatGPT integration, AI ethics), innovation programs (IMLS grants, the ALA Center for the Future of Libraries, Library Lab, Knight Foundation grants), emerging technologies (VR/AR, 3D printing, robotics, IoT, blockchain, voice assistants), future library space design, Library of Things programs, streaming services (Kanopy, Hoopla, OverDrive), gamification, libraries in the metaverse, the most innovative libraries in America, and global trends (Singapore, Finland, Denmark, South Korea, Netherlands). Compiled from verified web research (Wikipedia, ALA, IMLS, Knight Foundation, vendor press) and previously verified summary files in this data directory.

ai_in_libraries.overview: Artificial intelligence moved from the periphery to the mainstream of library operations between 2022 and 2025. The release of ChatGPT in November 2022 catalyzed library experimentation, the ALA Center for the Future of Libraries tracks 'Artificial Intelligence' as one of its core trend cards, and major library vendors (OCLC, EBSCO, ProQuest, Clarivate, OverDrive) embedded AI into cataloging, discovery, and reader engagement products. Libraries are simultaneously enthusiastic about efficiency gains and cautious about bias, copyright, hallucination, and patron-privacy risks.

applications.description: Libraries and their vendors deploy chatbots to answer frequently asked questions (hours, locations, card applications, hold status) 24/7. Some academic libraries (e.g., North Carolina State University Libraries' 'Ask the Librarian' service) and public systems have piloted ChatGPT-style assistants on their websites. The ALA tracks chatbots under both its 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'Robots' trend cards.
applications.status: Widespread pilots; vendor-embedded production use growing
examples: NC State University Libraries virtual assistant pilots
San Jose Public University and public-library consortial chatbots
Vendor chatbots on discovery layers (Primo, Summon, WorldCat Discovery)
applications.source: ALA Center for the Future of Libraries (Artificial Intelligence trend card); Wikipedia 'Chatbot'

applications.description: AI-assisted cataloging uses machine-learning models to suggest subject headings, generate Dewey/LC call numbers, classify resources, deduplicate records, and enrich bibliographic metadata. OCLC has applied AI to collection management and metadata quality, and Clarivate/ProQuest use AI in indexing and abstracting. The Library of Congress has experimented with machine-learning subject suggestion.
applications.status: Vendor production; ongoing experimentation at LC and large research libraries
examples: Clarivate machine-learning indexing in Web of Science
Library of Congress Labs machine-readable subject experiments
Backstage Library Works AI-assisted retrospective conversion
applications.source: library_tech_vendors_summary.json; ALA Center for the Future of Libraries

applications.description: Discovery layers increasingly use semantic search, vector retrieval, and large language models to surface relevant results beyond exact keyword matches. EBSCO's EBSCO Discovery Service, Ex Libris Primo, and ProQuest Summon have all added AI relevance tuning; several vendors launched generative-AI search assistants in 2023-2025 that summarize results for patrons.
examples: EBSCO EDS AI relevance tuning and 2024 generative search pilots
Ex Libris Primo AI relevancy and generative summaries

applications.description: After ChatGPT's November 2022 release, libraries began publishing generative-AI usage guidance, piloting ChatGPT for readers' advisory and reference triage, and integrating generative models into research guides. The ALA's Center for the Future of Libraries issued guidance and the Association of College & Research Libraries (ACRL) published frameworks on AI literacy. Many libraries added 'AI literacy' programming for patrons in 2024-2025.
examples: ALA / ACRL AI-literacy guidance and programming
University of Rhode Island 'AI Lab' (first academic-library AI lab in the U.S., opened 2018)
Public-library ChatGPT workshops (e.g., Skokie, Charlotte Mecklenburg)
Generative-AI reader's-advisory pilots in several urban systems
applications.source: ALA Center for the Future of Libraries; ACRL; American Libraries magazine

applications.description: Libraries are scrutinizing AI for bias, copyright infringement (training-data provenance), hallucinated citations, surveillance, and patron-privacy risks. The ALA, the Library Freedom Project, and IFLA have issued statements emphasizing human oversight, transparency, opt-in data use, and intellectual-freedom safeguards. Key concerns: AI-generated fake citations in student work, license terms that allow vendor training on patron queries, and inequitable access to premium AI tools.
key_concerns: Algorithmic bias in discovery ranking and recommendations
Patron-query privacy and vendor data retention
Digital divide in access to premium generative-AI tools
applications.source: ALA Center for the Future of Libraries; Library Freedom Project; IFLA Statement on Libraries and Artificial Intelligence

ai_in_libraries.ala_trend_card: The ALA Center for the Future of Libraries publishes a dedicated 'Artificial Intelligence' trend card alongside related cards for 'Robots,' 'Anonymity,' 'Privacy Shifting,' 'Data Everywhere,' and 'Facial Recognition,' signaling that AI is treated as a cluster of intersecting trends rather than a single technology.

imls_grants.overview: The Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS) is the primary federal funder of library innovation. IMLS is an independent agency established in 1996 under the Museum and Library Services Act, with a fiscal-year 2023 budget of $313.58 million and approximately 70 employees. The Office of Library Services offers five funding opportunities: National Leadership Grants for Libraries, Native American Library Services Basic and Enhancement Grants, Native Hawaiian Library Services Grants, and the Laura Bush 21st Century Librarian Program. About 1,500 Grants to States projects run each year under the Library Services and Technology Act (LSTA).

key_programs.purpose: Support projects that address significant challenges and opportunities facing the library field and that have the potential to advance practice in the profession.
key_programs.innovation_focus: AI, digital inclusion, makerspaces, accessibility, community engagement
key_programs.source: Wikipedia 'Institute of Museum and Library Services'; imls.gov

key_programs.purpose: Small grants (historically up to ~$50,000) to test and evaluate innovative, potentially transformative ideas in library services. Fayetteville Free Library's 2011 makerspace was seeded by a Sparks! Ignition grant.
key_programs.innovation_focus: Pilot projects, prototypes, novel service models
key_programs.source: Wikipedia 'Institute of Museum and Library Services'; library_makerspaces_summary.json

key_programs.purpose: Support developing a diverse workforce of librarians to meet the changing learning and information needs of the American public, including training in AI, data science, and emerging technologies.

The largest IMLS program by volume: ~1,500 projects/year administered by State Library Administrative Agencies (SLAAs) on themes including digital inclusion, climate change, and addressing historic inequities.
key_programs.innovation_focus: Broadband, digital literacy, hotspot lending, STEAM
key_programs.source: Wikipedia 'Institute of Museum and Library Services'

imls_grants.current_leadership_note: IMLS leadership has been in flux; Keith Sonderling is listed as Acting Director as of 2023-era sources, reflecting the agency's exposure to political transitions and the 2025 effort to dismantle the agency.

ala_center_for_the_future_of_libraries.overview: The ALA Center for the Future of Libraries, hosted by the American Library Association, is the profession's foresight and trend-tracking hub. It maps societal, technological, and demographic trends to library practice through trend cards, a Future of Libraries Fellowship, an Advisory Group, newsletters, and the annual Symposium on the Future of Libraries.
offerings: Trend Cards (40+ trends mapped to library implications)
Symposium on the Future of Libraries (annual)
Advisory Group of practitioners and futurists

library_lab.overview: The term 'Library Lab' denotes innovation labs embedded in or serving libraries. Two notable senses exist: (1) the Harvard Library Innovation Lab (LIL), a software-development team inside Harvard Library that builds open-source tools for libraries (including StackLife, the Caselaw Access Project, and Perma.cc, a service that archives cited web pages for legal scholarship); and (2) 'library lab' as a generic label for in-library experimentation spaces that overlap with makerspaces.
harvard_lil_projects: Caselaw Access Project (digitized U.S. case law, open access)
Library Cloud and open metadata work
library_lab.generic_use: Many public and academic libraries brand their digital experimentation or maker spaces as 'labs' (e.g., NC State University Libraries' makerspace ecosystem, Allen County Public Library Maker Labs, the Library of Congress Labs).
library_lab.source: Wikipedia 'Library of Congress Labs'; library_makerspaces_summary.json; lil.law.harvard.edu

knight_foundation_grants.overview: The John S. and James L. Knight Foundation, a private independent foundation founded in December 1950 and headquartered in Miami, Florida, focuses on journalism, arts, research, and community development. Its endowment was $2.5 billion in 2023. Through open competitions, Knight has funded library innovation, most notably the Knight News Challenge on Libraries.

knight_news_challenge_on_libraries.description: A multi-year open-competition grant program that asked 'How might libraries serve 21st-century information needs?' It funded projects connecting libraries to internet access, open data, civic technology, and digital services. The News Challenge model itself began in 2006 as a fund for projects improving how communities access news and information.
funded_themes: Open data and civic-tech partnerships with libraries
Digital inclusion and internet access through libraries
related_programs: Knight News Challenge (est. 2006, digital news/information projects)
Knight Arts Challenge ($20 million, South Florida arts, 2008)

knight_foundation_grants.founded: December 1950 (originally Charles L. Knight Memorial Education Fund, 1940)

emerging_tech.overview: Beyond books, U.S. libraries are adopting an expanding portfolio of emerging technologies. The ALA Center for the Future of Libraries explicitly tracks many of these as trend cards (Internet of Things, Robots, Drones, Self-Driving Cars, Haptic Technology, Facial Recognition, Blockchain). 3D printing is the most widespread maker technology, with an estimated 500-700 public libraries offering it.

technologies.description: Libraries lend VR headsets (Meta Quest, HTC Vive) and run VR programs for education, job training, travel, and accessibility. AR is used for wayfinding and to overlay historical context onto physical spaces. Academic libraries use VR for immersive research and simulation.
technologies.status: Growing; headsets lent at dozens of public systems
examples: State Library of Queensland 'The Edge' digital makerspace (VR/AR)
Academic-library VR labs (NC State, University of Oklahoma)

technologies.description: The flagship maker technology: an estimated 500-700 U.S. public libraries offer 3D printing. Fayetteville Free Library (NY) launched the first public-library makerspace in 2011; Chicago Public Library opened its Innovation Lab Maker Lab in 2013 with 3D printers, a milling machine, and laser cutters, winning the Chicago Innovation Awards Social Innovator Award.
technologies.source: library_makerspaces_summary.json; Wikipedia 'Chicago Public Library'; Pew Research 2016

technologies.description: Robots in libraries range from book-delivery robots (Helsinki Oodi's robots transport books to the third floor) to humanoid service robots and telepresence units. The ALA tracks 'Robots' as a dedicated trend card; some libraries use robotics kits (LEGO Mindstorms, NAO) in STEAM programming.
examples: Helsinki Central Library Oodi book-transport robots
technologies.source: Wikipedia 'Helsinki Central Library Oodi'; ALA 'Robots' trend card

technologies.description: Library buildings use IoT sensors for occupancy counting, environmental monitoring (temperature, humidity, CO2 for collection preservation), smart lighting, and space utilization analytics. The ALA Center for the Future of Libraries tracks 'Internet of Things' as a trend card.
technologies.source: ALA 'Internet of Things' trend card; library tech trade press

technologies.description: ALA's Center for the Future of Libraries funded research and published a 'Blockchain' trend card exploring uses such as provenance for digital collections, interlibrary-loan tracking, credentialing, and decentralized catalog infrastructure. San Jose State University's iSchool led an IMLS-funded investigation of blockchain applications for information services.
technologies.status: Research and pilot stage; not widely deployed
technologies.source: ALA 'Blockchain' trend card; IMLS National Leadership Grant to SJSU iSchool

technologies.description: Libraries pilot voice-assistant skills on Amazon Alexa and Google Assistant for catalog search, hold placement, and event information. The ALA tracks 'Connected Toys' and voice-interface implications for children and accessibility.
examples: Library Alexa skills (e.g., due-date and catalog queries)
Voice-assisted accessibility services for visually impaired patrons
technologies.source: ALA 'Connected Toys' and 'Artificial Intelligence' trend cards

future_spaces.overview: The future library is being redesigned around flexibility, creation, and community use rather than book storage. As collections move to shared off-site and digital storage, floor space is reallocated to collaborative, maker, and media-production uses. The ALA Center for the Future of Libraries tracks 'Co-Working / Co-Living' and 'Experiential Retail' as trends shaping library space.

space_types.description: Movable walls, modular furniture, and power/data in the floor allow libraries to reconfigure a single room between lecture, study, performance, and event modes. Examples include Salt Lake City Public Library's 'Urban Room' foyer spanning five floors under a 20,000-sq-ft skylight.
examples: Salt Lake City Public Library Urban Room
space_types.source: Wikipedia 'Salt Lake City Public Library'; library_makerspaces_summary.json

space_types.description: Libraries provide free or low-cost co-working environments with Wi-Fi, power, meeting rooms, and business resources, serving remote workers, freelancers, and small-business owners. The ALA explicitly tracks 'Co-Working / Co-Living' as a trend card.

Sound-treated recording booths with microphones, mixing boards, cameras, and editing software let patrons produce music, voiceovers, and video. Audio/video production is the fastest-growing maker category.
examples: Allen County Public Library media studios (Fort Wayne, IN)
Skokie Public Library digital media lab

space_types.description: Dedicated podcast booths have proliferated since ~2018, lowering barriers for community storytelling and civic journalism. Many are bookable by cardholders at no cost.
examples: Chicago Public Library YOUmedia and maker audio
Public-library podcast booths nationwide (Skokie, Sacramento, etc.)

space_types.description: Spaces equipped with VR/AR headsets, driving or medical simulators, and screen-based training environments for career and life-skills simulation (job interviews, public-speaking, technical training).
Demonstration kitchens for culinary-literacy programming, nutrition classes, and community events. Fayetteville Public Library (AR) added a teaching kitchen in its 2021 expansion.

library_of_things.overview: A Library of Things lends non-traditional items beyond books. The concept has historical precedents (St. Louis, MO, lent tennis rackets and board games as early as 1894). The term 'Library of Things' was popularized in the UK by a 2014 London grassroots experiment inspired by the Toronto Tool Library; in the U.S., a Sacramento, California librarian independently devised a similar idea and the same name in 2013, attracting media coverage and inspiring copycats.
common_categories: Arts and crafts (sewing machines, knitting kits, die-cutters)
Electronics and technology (Arduino, Makey Makey, Raspberry Pi, robotics kits, coding toys)
Kitchen equipment (food dehydrators, popcorn machines, ice cream makers, air fryers, instant pots, stand mixers)
Home tools (hand and power tools; Kill A Watt electricity meters; thermal cameras; leak detectors)
Recreation (telescopes, fishing poles, sports gear, board games, cake pans, novelty bakeware)
Science and maker (digital microscopes, telescopes, light meters, science kits, 3D printers, laser cutters)
Cultural and civic (museum and attraction passes, State Park passes)

programs.items: Seeds, tools, kitchen equipment, and other non-traditional items
programs.significance: U.S. pioneer; the Sacramento librarian coined 'Library of Things' in 2013, inspiring copycats nationwide.

programs.library: Berkeley Public Library Tool Lending Library
programs.items: Hand and power tools for home improvement, construction, and fine woodworking
programs.significance: One of the oldest U.S. tool-lending libraries, exemplifying the access-over-ownership model.

programs.items: Art prints, instruments, tools, science kits, and unusual items
programs.significance: Listed among notable U.S. Library-of-Things programs; lends art prints and instruments.

programs.items: Non-traditional lending collection
programs.significance: Cited among notable U.S. Library-of-Things programs.

programs.items: Non-traditional items
programs.significance: Listed among notable U.S. Library-of-Things programs.

programs.items: Non-traditional items
programs.significance: Listed among notable U.S. Library-of-Things programs.

programs.library: Richmond Public Library (Richmond Grows Seed Lending Library)
programs.items: Heirloom and vegetable seeds; patrons borrow, grow, save, and return seed
programs.significance: Called the 'unofficial spiritual center' of the public-library seed-library movement.

programs.items: Heirloom seeds
programs.significance: The first seed library established in a U.S. public library (2004, developed by Ken Greene).

programs.items: Locally adapted heirloom seeds
programs.significance: The United States' oldest seed library; grew from the Berkeley Ecology Center.

programs.items: Heirloom and locally adapted seeds
programs.significance: Prominent community seed-sharing organization with monthly checkouts.

programs.significance: One of the earliest and largest U.S. hotspot-lending programs, funded partly by philanthropic grants.

programs.items: Mobile WiFi hotspots; maker equipment via Innovation Lab
programs.significance: Early municipal hotspot lender; Innovation Lab Maker Lab (2013) won Chicago Innovation Award.

programs.items: Kill A Watt electricity-use meters and home-monitoring tools (thermal cameras, leak detectors, air-quality meters, infrared thermometers)
programs.significance: Notable for lending energy-monitoring tools that help patrons cut utility bills.

programs.library: Allen County Public Library Maker Labs
programs.items: 3D printers, maker equipment, media production tools
programs.significance: Main Library and Georgetown branch host Maker Labs; also runs a public-access TV station (Access Fort Wayne).

programs.items: Seeds and specialized kitchen equipment
programs.significance: Operates both a seed library and kitchen-equipment lending; the dual program is frequently cited.

programs.items: Maker equipment and non-traditional lending across branches
programs.significance: Multi-branch Kansas system listed among notable Library-of-Things programs.

programs.items: Digital media lab equipment, digitization tools, non-traditional items
programs.significance: Noted for digital media lab, digitization services, and innovation programming.

programs.items: 3D printers, fabrication tools, audio equipment
programs.significance: Opened the first U.S. public-library makerspace (~2011, conceived by Lauren Britton), seeding the maker-and-Things movement.

programs.items: Hand and power tools
programs.significance: International inspiration for the 'Library of Things' term; inspired the 2014 London Library of Things.

programs.items: Household and occasional-use items
programs.significance: Grassroots 2014 experiment that popularized the term 'Library of Things' globally.

library_of_things.seed_library_count_note: The Seed Library Social Network and library_sustainability_summary.json estimate 500+ U.S. seed libraries as of the mid-2020s, often supported by Master Gardener and Cooperative Extension partners.

streaming_services.overview: Library streaming has become a core digital service. Public libraries offer feature films, documentaries, television, and instructional video through vendor platforms, and an increasing number produce their own streaming content (recorded author talks, storytimes, local-history archives, civic meetings).

services.type: Streaming video for libraries and universities
services.owner: OverDrive (a KKR portfolio company; acquired Kanopy July 15, 2021)
services.founded: December 25, 2008, in Scarborough, Western Australia; HQ San Francisco, CA
services.model: Each participating public library, college, and university gets a customizable website. Patrons stream films, TV, documentaries, and educational videos using monthly play credits; the library pays per play.
services.content: Films, documentaries, TV shows, educational videos, The Great Courses, Kanopy Kids
services.features: Captions, transcripts, watchlists, customized portals per institution

services.type: Multi-format streaming/lending (video, audio, ebooks, comics, music)
services.owner: Midwest Tape (parent founded 1989 by John Eldred and Jeff Jankowski; Hoopla launched 2013)
services.model: Library cardholders borrow and stream with no holds and no waiting. Introduced Hoopla Flex (2020) to move one-copy/one-user titles, BingePass (2021, seven-day access to entire collections with one borrow), and SeasonPass (January 2025, borrow an entire TV season with one borrow). Broadcasts in standard definition.
services.content: Audiobooks, eBooks, comics, manga, music, movies, TV shows
services.scale: 6.5 million library card holders and 2,700+ library partners (2020 figure)

services.owner: OverDrive (acquired by KKR from Rakuten in 2020)
services.scale: 92,000 libraries and schools served; 100 countries; 600 million annual digital checkouts (2023)
services.model: One-copy/one-user lending withholds; Libby app launched 2017 for consumer-friendly reading and listening. OverDrive video has been de-emphasized as Kanopy (now an OverDrive subsidiary) consolidates streaming video.

services.description: Libraries increasingly produce their own streaming content: recorded author talks and lectures, virtual storytimes (expanded massively during COVID-19), local-history and oral-history archives, civic-meeting recordings, podcasts, and copyrighted local-history documentaries. Platforms include YouTube, library websites, and DPLA/HathiTrust for digitized collections.
examples: Nashville Public Library puppet-show videos and digital collections
Virtual storytimes recorded nationwide during COVID-19 (2020-2021)
Local-history and oral-history archives on library YouTube channels and DPLA

gamification.overview: Gamification is the integration of game-design elements (points, badges, leaderboards, progress bars, levels, avatars, and meaningful stories) into non-game contexts to increase engagement and motivation. The ALA Center for the Future of Libraries tracks 'Gamification' and 'Badging' as distinct trend cards. Libraries apply gamification to summer reading, lifelong learning, information-literacy instruction, and STEM programs.
mechanics: Points (earned for reading, completing programs, visiting branches)
Badges (digital credentials for milestones; ALA tracks 'Badging' trend)

applications.description: Most U.S. public libraries (95% offer summer reading per ALA Digital Inclusion / programming surveys) run gamified summer reading programs where children, teens, and adults log minutes or books to earn points, badges, and prizes. Platforms like READsquared, Beanstack, and Scholastic's summer-reading tools formalize the points-and-badge model.
applications.source: library_innovation_enhanced_summary.json (95% offer summer reading); Gamification Wikipedia

applications.description: Libraries issue digital badges for completing information-literacy tutorials, coding workshops, and digital-literacy modules. The ALA tracks 'Badging' as a trend card; Chicago Public Library's Learning Circles and YOUmedia have used badging.
applications.source: ALA 'Badging' trend card; Chicago Public Library YOUmedia

applications.description: Some libraries reward reading with points redeemable for raffle entries, fine forgiveness, or community-donation matches (e.g., 'Read Down Your Fines' programs gamify reading to clear cardholder debt).

Libraries build physical or digital escape rooms - timed puzzle-solving challenges - to teach information literacy, orientation, and subject content. Escape rooms originated in Asia in the late 2000s (first fixed-location rooms opened in Asia, then Hungary, Serbia, Australia, New Zealand, and Russia in the early 2010s) and spread to North America, Europe, and East Asia through the 2010s. Library escape rooms typically require teams to solve catalog, citation, or primary-source puzzles to 'escape.'
examples: Public-library Halloween and summer-reading-themed escape rooms
Digital escape rooms built in Google Forms / Breakout EDU

gamification.caveats: Gamification critics warn of over-justification (extrinsic rewards crowding out intrinsic reading motivation), equity issues when prizes favor affluent participants, and data-privacy concerns when patron reading behavior is tracked and scored.

metaverse_vr.overview: A metaverse is a collective 3D virtual shared space in which users, represented as avatars, interact socially and economically. The term gained mainstream attention when Facebook renamed itself Meta Platforms in 2021 and committed to building the metaverse; Meta's social VR world, launched as Facebook Horizon in 2019, was rebranded Horizon Worlds. Libraries have begun experimenting with metaverse and VR presences, virtual branch buildings, and 3D digital collections.

library_approaches.approach: Virtual library branches in social VR
library_approaches.description: Libraries have prototyped virtual branches in platforms like VRChat, Second Life (the original avatar-based virtual world still in operation), Mozilla Hubs, and Meta Horizon Worlds, hosting author talks, exhibitions, and reference services accessible from anywhere.

Libraries digitize special collections into 3D models and VR exhibits, letting remote patrons 'walk through' historical spaces or examine artifacts in immersive VR. Academic libraries lead here, often in partnership with campus VR labs.
examples: Library of Congress 3D/VR digital collections pilots
Academic-library VR exhibits of special collections
Public-library VR field trips and travel programs

library_approaches.description: Libraries lend VR headsets (Meta Quest, HTC Vive) and run group VR programs for education, fitness, accessibility, and senior engagement (e.g., travel VR for homebound patrons).
examples: State Library of Queensland 'The Edge' VR/AR

challenges: Accessibility for users with motion sensitivity or disabilities
Vendor lock-in to proprietary metaverse platforms
Patron safety, moderation, and harassment in social VR
Privacy and biometric data from VR headsets
Sustainability after early pilots (Microsoft shut AltspaceVR in March 2023)
metaverse_vr.status: Early and uneven. Most activity is pilot-stage in a subset of well-resourced public and academic libraries; the field contracted after the 2022-2023 metaverse hype cycle cooled and several platforms (AltspaceVR) shut down.

innovative_libraries.innovation: Opened the first U.S. public-library makerspace (~2011, conceived by Lauren Britton Smedley, seeded by an IMLS Sparks! Ignition grant). Pioneered the maker movement in public libraries.

2021 expansion brought total size to 170,500 sq ft and added an event center seating 700+, an innovation center, a teaching kitchen, an art and movement room, and dedicated teen spaces. LEED-certified (2004 main building).

Opened its Innovation Lab in June 2013 with a Maker Lab (3D software, milling machine, laser cutters, 3D printers), winning the Chicago Innovation Awards Social Innovator Award in October 2013. Same month announced a $1 million Gates Foundation grant partnering CPL with the Aarhus, Denmark public library system. Pioneered YOUmedia teen digital-media spaces and launched One Book, One Chicago.

U.S. pioneer of the Library of Things (2013), lending seeds, tools, and kitchen equipment; 28 branches. The Sacramento librarian's program attracted substantial media coverage and inspired nationwide copycats.

One of the earliest and largest mobile-hotspot lending programs, lending cellular WiFi hotspots to households without home internet, funded partly by philanthropic grants. Pioneered large-scale digital-inclusion lending.

Moshe Safdie-designed main library opened February 8, 2003: a five-story, 240,000-sq-ft building with a curved five-story glass wall, a 20,000-sq-ft skylight over the 'Urban Room' foyer, and a rooftop garden with beehives. A landmark in future-oriented, experiential library architecture.

Rem Koolhaas / Joshua Prince-Ramus (OMA) with LMN Architects designed the Seattle Central Library, opened 2004 - an internationally influential diamond-glass-and-steel building that redefined the modern library as a civic icon. Holds 1.8 million physical items as of 2023; the seventh-floor ZAPP Zine Collection holds 30,000+ zines.

Rebranded 'Anythink' in 2009; pioneered the experiential library model and the BiblioCommons-style discovery experience. The Studio at Anythink Wright connects making to nature and sustainability; recipient of IMLS National Leadership grants.

Main Library and Georgetown branch host Maker Labs; the system operates Access Fort Wayne (a full public-access TV production facility with two studios), an Audio Reading Service (founded 1979), and community radio station WELT 95.7 FM - a rare library-media hybrid.

Operates a digital media lab, digitization services, VR lending, and innovative programming; frequently cited as a model suburban library for early adoption of digital-media production and digitization services.

innovative_libraries.library: ImaginOn: The Joe and Joan Martin Center
innovative_libraries.innovation: A 102,000-sq-ft landmark youth library and theatre, a collaboration of Charlotte Mecklenburg Library and Children's Theatre of Charlotte, opened October 8, 2005. Houses Tech Central, the Loft (teen space), Studio I, the Spangler Children's Library, McColl Family Theatre, and Wells Fargo Playhouse - a national model for combining library and performing-arts space for youth.

Main Library plus 22 branches; 1,483,433-item collection and 13.1 million annual circulation. Recognized for service innovation including Ready for Kindergarten programming, extensive ESL programming for growing Hispanic and Somali populations, and Spanish-language technology classes.

Operates Studio NPL (a teen digital-media studio network), puppet-show programming at Main and across branches, digital collections and language-learning services, and 'Be Well at NPL' wellness programming. Received a National Institutes of Health / National Library of Medicine community-engagement award for health-literacy work.

A 501(c)(3) non-profit community technology center and digital library opened November 2015 in a repurposed Borders Bookstore, with Apple/Windows/Ubuntu computers, tablets, laptops, and a 3D lab (3D printers, 3D scanners, laser cutter). Services are free to the public except for expendables; began occupying the second floor of the new Omaha Central Library in April 2026.
Multi-branch system recognized for civic innovation and Library-of-Things programming across its branches; listed among notable U.S. Library-of-Things programs.

innovative_libraries.library: University of Rhode Island Libraries (AI Lab)
innovative_libraries.innovation: Opened what is widely cited as the first academic-library AI lab in the United States (2018), providing students hands-on access to AI tools and workshops - an early model for AI literacy programming in libraries.
innovative_libraries.source: ALA Center for the Future of Libraries; ACRL

innovative_libraries.innovation: The Library of Congress digital innovation lab experiments with machine-readable subject access, crowdsourced transcription (By the People), AI-assisted metadata, and large-scale digitization - anchoring federal innovation in the library field.

global_trends.overview: The National Library Board is a statutory board established 1 September 1995 under Singapore's Ministry of Digital Development and Information, headquartered at the National Library Building, 100 Victoria Street. NLB's 2025 annual budget is S$332.06 million. Singapore integrates its library system into the national 'Smart Nation' strategy, emphasizing digital services, mobile apps, and self-service technology.
innovations: NLB Mobile app for catalog, borrowing, and e-services
Self-service kiosks and automated returns across the network
Smart-Nation integration of libraries into national digital infrastructure
Extensive digital collections and e-resources

global_trends.lead_institution: Helsinki Central Library Oodi (Helsinki City Library)
global_trends.overview: Oodi, the Helsinki Central Library, was inaugurated 5 December 2018 on the eve of Finnish Independence Day, adjacent to Finlandia Hall and the Museum of Contemporary Art. Designed by ALA Architects (won over 543 competitors), it cost an estimated EUR 98 million (the state paid EUR 30 million as a centenary project). In 2019 the International Federation of Library Associations (IFLA) named Oodi the best Public Library of the Year.
innovations: Three-story design with only ~100,000 books on the third floor; the rest is events and meetings
Specially designed robots transport books to the third floor
Ultimaker 3D printers and a maker/urban workshop on the second floor
Sewing-machine and equipment lending
Kino Regina cinema (run by the National Audiovisual Institute KAVI)
Smart-glass meeting rooms
global_trends.award: IFLA Public Library of the Year 2019

global_trends.overview: Dokk1 is a library and culture center in Aarhus, completed in 2015 and designed by Schmidt Hammer Lassen Architects. The 60,000-sqm (650,000-sq-ft), four-floor building sits on the harbour and features a glass prism making activities visible from outside, automated parking for 1,000 cars, a robotic book-and-media delivery system, and an Urban Mediaspace. Dokk1 developed a library- innovation tool kit supported by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation Global Libraries program, and partnered with Chicago Public Library via a 2013 $1 million Gates grant.
innovations: Robotic book-and-media delivery system
Automated parking for 1,000 cars
Urban Mediaspace concept exported globally via Gates Foundation-supported tool kit
CPL-Aarhus partnership (2013, $1M Gates Foundation grant)

global_trends.overview: The National Library of Korea, in Banpo-dong, Seocho-gu, Seoul, was established 15 October 1945 (80 years as of 2025). It holds 12,768,751 items (9,158,363 Korean-language books, 1,552,489 foreign-language books, 1,771,738 non-book items, 286,161 old texts) and an extensive digital collection of newspapers and primary sources on Korean history, many freely available online. Director: Suh Hye Ran. South Korea pairs this with aggressive national digital-library investment and smart-library pilots.
innovations: Extensive freely accessible digital newspaper and primary-source archives
National digital-library platform investment
Smart-library pilots with self-service and automation
Legal deposit under the Library Act (Article 20)

global_trends.lead_institution: Koninklijke Bibliotheek (KB), National Library of the Netherlands
global_trends.overview: The KB in The Hague was established in 1798 (228 years as of 2026) and holds about 7 million printed items (over 115 km / 71 mi of books), serving as the national deposit library. Director: Wilma van Wezenbeek; 481 FTE employees (2023). The KB runs major national digital services: the national online Library (e-books and audiobooks), Delpher (millions of digitized pages), and The Memory (about 800,000 images). Since 2015 the KB has played a leading role in the national public-library network.
innovations: Delpher - millions of digitized newspaper, book, and magazine pages
The Memory (Het Geheugen) - about 800,000 digitized images
National online Library with e-books and audiobooks
National public-library network leadership since 2015
STCN (Short-Title Catalogue, Netherlands) retrospective bibliography
global_trends.collection_size_printed: about 7 million items (115 km of books)

key_findings: AI moved to the center of library innovation after ChatGPT's November 2022 release: the ALA Center for the Future of Libraries tracks AI as a core trend card, and major vendors (OCLC, EBSCO, ProQuest, Clarivate, OverDrive) have embedded AI into cataloging, discovery, and reader engagement by 2023-2025.

The ALA Center for the Future of Libraries is the profession's foresight hub, mapping 40+ trends (Artificial Intelligence, Blockchain, Gamification, Internet of Things, Robots, Co-Working, Sharing Economy, Subscription Boxes, etc.) to library practice through trend cards, a fellowship, and an annual Symposium on the Future of Libraries.

IMLS is the primary federal innovation funder: a $313.58 million FY2023 budget across National Leadership Grants, Sparks! Ignition Grants, the Laura Bush 21st Century Librarian Program, and ~1,500 annual LSTA Grants to States - seeding landmarks like the Fayetteville Free Library makerspace (2011).

Library of Things programs, sparked by a Sacramento librarian's 2013 idea (the term itself was popularized in the UK in 2014), now span tool, seed, kitchen, instrument, toy, hotspot, and energy-monitor lending - with 500+ U.S. seed libraries alone.

Streaming is a core library service: Kanopy (founded 2008, acquired by OverDrive in 2021) and Hoopla Digital (launched 2013 by Midwest Tape of Holland, OH; 2,700+ library partners and 6.5 million cardholders as of 2020) deliver films, TV, music, audiobooks, ebooks, and comics to cardholders.

Helsinki's Oodi (opened 5 December 2018; IFLA Public Library of the Year 2019) and Aarhus's Dokk1 (opened 2015; robotic book delivery, 1,000-car automated parking) are the global benchmarks for future library space, with book-transport robots and only ~100,000 books on Oodi's top floor - the rest devoted to events and making.

Gamification is mainstream in U.S. libraries: 95% of public libraries run summer reading programs, now routinely gamified via Beanstack, READsquared, and badge systems, and library escape rooms (built on a format that spread globally in the 2010s) teach information literacy through timed puzzle-solving.

Future library space is being redefined around flexible, maker, and media uses: Chicago Public Library's 2013 Innovation Lab Maker Lab, Fayetteville (AR)'s 2021 teaching kitchen and innovation center, and Allen County Public Library's TV studios and radio station exemplify the shift from book storage to community creation.

The metaverse and VR movement reached libraries during the 2021 Meta rebranding hype, but the field contracted as platforms consolidated - Microsoft shut AltspaceVR in March 2023 - leaving mostly pilot-stage VR lending and 3D-collection exhibits in well-resourced public and academic libraries.

Knight Foundation (founded December 1950; $2.5 billion endowment in 2023; HQ Miami) funded library innovation through the Knight News Challenge on Libraries, an open competition asking how libraries can serve 21st-century information needs, building on the News Challenge model launched in 2006.

Singapore's National Library Board (est. 1995; S$332.06 million 2025 budget) integrates libraries into the national Smart Nation strategy, while the Netherlands' KB (est. 1798) runs Delpher (millions of digitized pages) and The Memory (~800,000 images) as national-scale digital library infrastructure.

Ethics is a first-order concern: the ALA, IFLA, and the Library Freedom Project emphasize that AI in libraries requires human oversight, training-data transparency, patron-query privacy, and safeguards against algorithmic bias and censorship-by-algorithm.

The 2024 FCC expansion of E-rate to off-premises hotspot lending - a landmark for digital-equity innovation - was reversed in October 2025 by a 2-1 FCC vote, illustrating that policy reversals can unwind library innovation faster than grants can build it.

Institute of Museum and Library Services (imls.gov) - grant programs, FY2023 budget $313.58M
Knight Foundation (knightfoundation.org) - News Challenge on Libraries; $2.5B endowment 2023
Harvard Library Innovation Lab (lil.law.harvard.edu) - Perma.cc, Caselaw Access Project

source.methodology: Facts were verified by fetching the cited Wikipedia and organization pages (HTTP 200) and extracting specific, attributable statements (founding dates, budgets, partner counts, program names, awards). Quantitative estimates (e.g., 500-700 libraries offering 3D printing; 500+ seed libraries) are inherited from previously verified summary files in this directory and are best-effort ranges, not registry counts. Where a single authoritative census does not exist (makerspaces, Library of Things counts), figures are flagged as estimates and should be re-verified against primary sources (ALA, IMLS, USGBC, Seed Library Social Network) before publication.

library_attitudes.title: Public Attitudes Toward Libraries: What Americans Think
library_attitudes.overview: Americans overwhelmingly value their public libraries. Majorities say libraries provide the resources they need, and two-thirds say closing their local library would have a major impact on their community. Yet despite this broad support, library visitation has been declining, particularly among younger and lower-income Americans. This section examines the gap between how Americans value libraries and how they actually use them, drawing on data from Pew Research Center, Gallup, and the NEA Survey of Public Participation in the Arts.

attitudes.description: Pew Research Center surveys consistently show that Americans hold libraries in high regard, with strong majorities saying libraries are essential community resources.

findings.finding: 77% say libraries provide the resources they need
66% say closing the library would have a major impact on the community
33% say closing the library would have a major impact on their family
69% say libraries contribute a lot as a safe place to spend time
58% say libraries contribute a lot to educational opportunities
49% say libraries spark creativity in young people
47% say libraries are trusted sources for tech learning
37% say libraries help people decide what information to trust

expectations.description: When asked what libraries should offer, Americans express strong expectations for digital and creative services.

reasons_for_use.description: Among Americans who visited a library in the past 12 months, book borrowing remains the most common activity, but program attendance is rising.

activities.activity: Sat, read, studied, or engaged with media

key_facts: 77% of Americans say libraries provide the resources they need (Pew 2016).
66% say closing their local public library would have a major impact on their community (Pew 2016), up from 63% in 2013.
69% say libraries contribute a lot as a safe place to spend time, and 58% say they provide educational opportunities.
80% of Americans say libraries should definitely teach digital skills, showing high expectations for library tech services.
Despite valuing libraries, only 31% say books should definitely not be moved to make room for tech spaces, while 24% support it and 40% are open to it.
Among recent library visitors, 64% checked out a printed book (down from 73% in 2012), while program attendance rose 10 points from 2015 to 2016.
Women visit libraries more often than men: 13.4 vs 7.5 visits per year (Gallup 2019).
Young adults (18-29) are the most frequent library visitors at 15.5 visits per year (Gallup 2019).
Lower-income Americans (<$40K) visit libraries more often (12.2 visits/yr) than higher-income ($100K+, 8.5 visits/yr).
Midwesterners visit libraries most often (12.9 visits/yr), while Southerners visit least (9.3 visits/yr).
College graduates are the most likely to have visited a library in the past year (59%), followed by women (57%) and parents (55%).
Among library tech users, 61% use library internet for school or work research, and 38% use it to acquire health information.

library_access_equity.title: Library Access Equity: Who Uses Libraries & Why It Matters
library_access_equity.overview: Public libraries are among the most equitably used institutions in American life, serving Americans across all racial, ethnic, and income groups at remarkably similar rates. The landmark US IMPACT Study (2010) found that 77 million Americans age 14+ used a library computer or wireless network in a single year, making libraries the nation's primary free internet access provider. During the Great Recession, libraries became essential job-seeking infrastructure, with 62% of unemployed Americans using libraries and 92% of libraries providing job resources. This section examines the equity of library access and the critical role libraries play in bridging digital, economic, and informational divides.

us_impact_study_2010.source: U.S. IMPACT Study 2010, Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, via ALA fact sheet
us_impact_study_2010.finding: Nearly one-third of Americans age 14+ used a public library computer or wireless network in the prior year.
us_impact_study_2010.significance: The US IMPACT Study, funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, was the first large-scale national study to document the critical role of public library computers and internet access in American life. It surveyed over 45,000 people across the US and found that library technology access was essential for education, employment, health, e-government, and social connection.

library_use_by_ethnicity.description: Library use in America is remarkably equitable across racial and ethnic groups. A 1997 study found that Asian/Pacific Islander Americans had the highest library use rate (72% in past year), with all other groups between 58-66%. NCES household data from 2002 showed similar rates of library use for school assignments across all racial groups (20-26%).

study_1997.source: 1997 American Libraries article, via ALA fact sheet

nces_2002.source: NCES, Households Use of Public and Other Types of Libraries (2002), via ALA fact sheet

libraries_and_jobs.description: During the Great Recession (2008-2012), libraries became essential job-seeking infrastructure. The ALA Public Library Funding & Technology Access Study (PLFTAS) documented the critical role libraries played in helping unemployed Americans find work, submit applications, and access government services.
key_findings: 92% of libraries provided job resources (PLFTAS 2011-12).
76% of libraries helped patrons with online job applications (PLFTAS 2011-12).
96% of libraries assisted with e-government services (PLFTAS 2011-12).
62% of unemployed Americans used the library to seek employment (PLFTAS 2009-10).
88% of libraries provided free access to job databases (PLFTAS 2009-10).
75% provided civil service exam materials (PLFTAS 2009-10).
69% provided resume software (PLFTAS 2009-10).
15% of libraries reduced operating hours during the recession, limiting access precisely when demand spiked (PLFTAS 2009-10).

computer_internet_access_by_race.description: The NCES 2002 household study revealed significant racial disparities in who uses library computers and internet. Black (13%), Hispanic (12%), and mixed-race (12%) Americans used library computers at higher rates than white non-Hispanic Americans (8%), suggesting that libraries serve as a critical digital access point for communities of color.
computer_internet_access_by_race.data_source: NCES, Households Use of Public and Other Types of Libraries (2002), via ALA fact sheet

key_facts: 77 million Americans age 14+ used a public library computer or wireless network in the prior year (US IMPACT Study 2010).
Nearly one-third (33%) of Americans age 14+ relied on library technology access (US IMPACT Study 2010).

Library use is remarkably equitable across racial groups: 72% of Asian/Pacific Islander Americans, 65% of white Americans, 63% of Black Americans, and 58% of Hispanic Americans used a library in the past year (1997 study).
53% of Asian/Pacific Islander Americans used a library in the past month, the highest rate of any racial group (1997 study).
Black Americans use library computers at a rate 63% higher than white Americans (13% vs 8%, NCES 2002).
During the Great Recession, 62% of unemployed Americans used libraries for job-seeking (PLFTAS 2009-10).
92% of public libraries provide job-seeking resources, making them the most widespread free job assistance infrastructure in the country (PLFTAS 2011-12).
96% of public libraries assist with e-government services, helping citizens navigate government programs online (PLFTAS 2011-12).
15% of libraries cut hours during the recession, reducing access at the exact moment demand was highest (PLFTAS 2009-10).
The US IMPACT Study was funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and surveyed over 45,000 Americans.
Library computer/internet use for school assignments was nearly equal across racial groups: Black 25%, Asian 26%, White 22%, Hispanic 20% (NCES 2002).
The PLFTAS (Public Library Funding & Technology Access Study) documented the critical intersection of library funding, technology access, and community need during 2009-2012.

reading_trends_enhanced.title: Reading & Library Visits: The Long Decline (NEA SPPA 2012-2022)
reading_trends_enhanced.overview: The NEA Survey of Public Participation in the Arts (SPPA) documents a troubling long-term decline in both reading and library visitation. Between 2012 and 2022, the percentage of Americans reading any book fell from 54.6% to 48.5%, while novel/short story reading dropped from 45.2% to 37.6%. Simultaneously, IMLS data shows library visits per capita fell from 3.85 in FY2019 to 2.53 in FY2024 — a 34% decline that predates but was accelerated by COVID-19. This section presents the year-by-year data from NEA and IMLS.

library_visits_trend.note: Pew measured 53% in-person visit rate (2012 peak)
NEA SPPA first measured library visits; lowest IMLS per-capita in series
Continued recovery but still ~34% below FY2019 per-capita

key_facts: The percentage of Americans reading any book declined from 54.6% in 2012 to 48.5% in 2022 — a 6.1 percentage point drop in a decade (NEA SPPA).
Novel and short story reading fell from 45.2% (2012) to 37.6% (2022), a decline of 7.6 points.
Poetry reading spiked to 11.7% in 2017 (up from 6.7% in 2012) before falling back to 9.2% in 2022.
Play reading has remained consistently low: 2.9% (2012), 3.7% (2017), 2.4% (2022).
IMLS per-capita library visits fell from 3.85 (FY2019) to 2.01 (FY2022) — a 48% decline — before partially recovering to 2.53 in FY2024.
Total IMLS library visits dropped from 1.25 billion (FY2019) to 732 million (FY2020) due to COVID-19 closures.
By FY2024, library visits recovered to 869 million but remained 34% below FY2019 per-capita levels.
Pew Research Center measured in-person library visit rate at 53% in 2012, declining to 44% by 2015 before recovering to 48% in 2016.
Gallup (2019) found Americans averaged 10.5 library visits per year, with young adults (18-29) visiting most at 15.5 times per year.
The NEA SPPA first measured public library visitation in 2022, finding a 23% visit rate.

special_libraries.title: Special Libraries & Mobile Services: Beyond the Public Library
special_libraries.overview: America's library ecosystem extends far beyond public library buildings. Special libraries serve specialized audiences — corporate libraries, law libraries, medical libraries, military libraries, and museum libraries. Bookmobiles bring library services to rural communities, nursing homes, and schools. Summer reading programs operate at 95% of public libraries. Friends of Libraries groups provide volunteer and financial support. This section covers the diverse types of libraries and services that make up the American library landscape.

special_libraries.description: A special library is a library that provides specialized information resources on a particular subject, serves a specialized and limited clientele, and delivers specialized services to that clientele. Special libraries include corporate libraries, government libraries, law libraries, medical libraries, museum libraries, military libraries, and news libraries. Special libraries also exist within academic institutions. These libraries are included as special libraries because they are often funded separately from the rest of the university and they serve a targeted group of users.

types.description: Libraries maintained by corporations for employees, containing industry-specific resources, market research, and technical documentation.
Libraries serving lawyers, judges, and law students, often attached to courts, law firms, or law schools.
Libraries in hospitals, medical schools, and health organizations providing specialized biomedical and clinical information.
Libraries at seminaries, religious institutions, and theological schools.
Libraries serving government agencies, including the Library of Congress, National Library of Medicine, and agency-specific libraries.
Libraries on military bases and in defense agencies, serving service members and their families worldwide.
Libraries within museums supporting curatorial research, exhibition development, and scholarly access to collections.
Libraries maintained by newspapers and media organizations, preserving archives and supporting journalistic research.

bookmobiles.description: A bookmobile, or mobile library, is a vehicle designed for use as a library. They have been known by many names throughout history, including traveling library, library wagon, book wagon, book truck, library-on-wheels, and book auto service. Bookmobiles expand the reach of traditional libraries by transporting books to potential readers, providing library services to people in otherwise underserved locations and/or circumstances. Bookmobile services and materials, may be customized for the locations and populations served.

history.event: Mary L. Titcomb, librarian at Washington County Free Library (MD), introduces the first American bookmobile — a wagon drawn by horses to deliver books to rural areas.
Motorized bookmobiles begin to replace horse-drawn wagons, dramatically expanding reach.
Library Services Act provides federal funding to extend library services to rural areas, accelerating bookmobile adoption.
Peak era of bookmobiles, with over 2,000 operating nationwide.
Bookmobile numbers begin declining as digital services and branch construction expand.
IMLS PLS FY2024 reports 767 bookmobiles still operating, serving rural and homebound populations.

bookmobiles.significance: Bookmobiles remain critical for reaching populations that cannot visit physical libraries: rural communities, nursing homes, schools without libraries, homebound individuals, and isolated populations.

summer_reading.description: Summer reading programs take place at 95% of public libraries in the United States. Children, teens, and adults participate in activities meant to encourage reading, such as keeping a reading log. Other names for summer reading programs include vacation reading club, summer reading club, vacation reading program, and summer library program.
summer_reading.significance: Summer reading programs combat the 'summer slide' — the loss of reading skills during school vacation. Research shows children who participate maintain or improve reading levels, with disproportionate benefits for low-income children.

friends_of_libraries.description: Friends of Libraries are non-profit, charitable groups formed to support libraries in their communities. Support from the Friends groups may be financial, political and cultural. Groups are separate from the libraries they support and made up of volunteers. Generally, groups are structured, handle finances and work closely with library management. In the United States, Friends groups also work closely with the American Library Association (ALA). Other countries, such as Australia, France, South Africa and the United Kingdom all have Friends of Libraries groups.
friends_of_libraries.role: Friends of Libraries groups are non-profit, charitable organizations that support libraries through fundraising, advocacy, volunteer work, and cultural programming.
activities: Used book sales — a primary fundraising activity generating millions nationally
Advocacy for library funding at local, state, and federal levels
Sponsoring author talks, book clubs, and cultural programs

american_library_association.description: The American Library Association (ALA) is a nonprofit organization based in the United States that promotes libraries and library education internationally. It is the oldest and largest library association in the world.
american_library_association.role: The ALA is the oldest and largest library association in the world. It accredits MLIS programs, sets professional standards, advocates for library funding and intellectual freedom, and publishes American Libraries magazine.

lsta.title: Library Services and Technology Act
lsta.description: United States President Bill Clinton signed the Library Services and Technology Act (LSTA) on October 1, 1996. LSTA is a United States federal library grant program. Its roots come from the Library Services Act, first enacted in 1956. LSTA replaced the Library Services and Construction Act (LSCA), first enacted in 1962. The National Commission on Libraries and Information Science held two White House Conferences that generated discussion and support.
lsta.significance: LSTA is the primary federal funding mechanism for libraries, administered by IMLS. It provides grants to states for library technology, services to underserved populations, and information access programs.

Kentucky leads the nation with 74 bookmobiles, followed by Ohio (68) and California (65).
The first American bookmobile was introduced in 1905 by Mary L. Titcomb at Washington County Free Library in Maryland, using a horse-drawn wagon.
95% of US public libraries offer summer reading programs, making them the most widespread library program in the country.
Special libraries include corporate, law, medical, theological, government, military, museum, and news libraries — each serving specialized audiences.
The American Library Association, founded in 1876, is the oldest and largest library association in the world.
The Library Services and Technology Act (LSTA), signed by President Clinton in 1996, is the primary federal funding mechanism for libraries.
LSTA replaced the Library Services and Construction Act (1962), which itself grew from the Library Services Act (1956).
Friends of Libraries groups are non-profit volunteer organizations that support libraries through fundraising, advocacy, and programming.

Summer reading programs combat the 'summer slide' with disproportionate benefits for low-income children.
The ALA accredits Master of Library and Information Science (MLIS) programs and sets professional standards for the field.

library_web_coverage.title: Library Online Presence: Website Coverage by State
library_web_coverage.overview: In an increasingly digital world, a library's website is its virtual front door. Yet website coverage varies dramatically by state. While some states have over 90% of libraries with discoverable websites, others have fewer than 15%, revealing a significant digital presence gap.
key_facts: 8,928 of 17,144 US libraries have a discoverable website — 52.1% national coverage.
The best-covered state is NH at 90.8%.
10 states have website coverage below 25%.
States with low website coverage tend to have many small, rural library systems.
The digital presence gap limits patron access to library services in low-coverage states.
Nationally, 52.1% of libraries have a discoverable website.

programs_2024_breakdown.overview: In FY2024, US public libraries hosted approximately 5.09M programs with 105M total attendance across 9,249 library systems. This breakdown reveals the shift toward virtual and off-site programming that began during COVID-19.

book_format_trend.title: Book Format Shift: Print, E-Books & Audiobooks (2011 vs 2025)
book_format_trend.overview: Over 14 years, Americans' reading format preferences shifted dramatically. Print declined from 72% to 64%, while e-books more than doubled from 17% to 31% and audiobooks more than tripled from 11% to 26%. Overall reading remained stable at ~75%.
key_facts: Print book readership declined from 72% (2011) to 64% (2025), an 8-point drop.
E-book readership more than doubled from 17% (2011) to 31% (2025).
Audiobook readership more than tripled from 11% (2011) to 26% (2025).
Overall reading remained stable at ~75%.
The e-book surge reflects Kindle, Libby/OverDrive, and library digital lending.
Audiobook growth is driven by smartphone apps and commute listening.
Print remains the dominant format at 64%.

nces_sass.overview: The NCES Schools and Staffing Survey (SASS) was the last comprehensive federal survey of school library media centers, discontinued after 2011-12. It provides a longitudinal view of school library infrastructure, staffing, and technology across four survey waves.

Average staff per media center declined from 1.89 (1999) to 1.77 (2011).
Certified specialists rose from 0.81 to 0.90 per center.
Automated catalog adoption jumped from 72.8% (1999) to 88.3% (2011).
The SASS was discontinued after 2011-12 — the last comprehensive federal school library survey.

national_snapshot.title: America's Libraries at a Glance: The National Snapshot (FY2024)
